text: Introducing Others

When you meet people, you will want to know how to introduce people other than yourself. This is very easy. You start with: Dit is ... (dit is) (This is...). Then you say the name of the person you introduce. You can clarify the relation by saying: Dit is Cilla Vermeent, de secretaresse van Hans van der Jagt (dit is si-la fer-mayn-t si-krer-taa-rehs-ser fan hans fan der yakh-t) (This is Cilla Vermeent, the secretary of Hans van der Jagt), or Dit is mijn collega Jessica de Rover (dit is mayn ko-lay-khaa yeh-see-kaa der roa-ver) (This is my colleague Jessica de Rover).

If you are introduced to an English-speaking person you probably will say: Nice to meet you. Elderly Dutch people will appreciate your using the sentence: Prettig met u kennis te maken (preh-tikh met uw keh-nis ter maa-kern) (Nice to meet you). When you are among younger and more informal people and you are introduced you just say Hallo and, while shaking hands, repeat your own name. Immediately after doing this you ask a question, for instance: Bent u een collega van Jacco Plooij? (bent uw erm ko-lay-khaa fan ya-kooa plooy) or, in more personal situations: Bent u een kennis van Jacco Plooij? (bent uw erm keh-nis fan ya-kooa plooy) (Are you an acquaintance of Jacco Plooij?). You address the person to whom you are introduced. Frequently the question regards the relation that the introduced person has to the person who introduced you to each other, but it can also concern the person you are introduced to: Bent u hier voor het eerst? (bent uw heer foar het ayrst) (Is this the first time that you are here?).
Introductions at special occasions
Occasionally you are in a situation where introducing and meeting are very formal. There are some sentences that work well:

phrases.dutch: Mag ik u voorstellen: Jessica de Rover.
phrases.pronunciation: mahk ik uw foar-steh-lern yeh-see-kaa der roa-ver
phrases.translation: May I introduce to you: Jessica de Rover.

phrases.dutch: Prettig met u kennis te maken.
phrases.pronunciation: preh-tikh met uw keh-nis ter maa-kern

text: Talkin' the Talk

In this dialogue a young director, Raymond van Dieren, meets an older director, Hans van der Jagt, on a formal occasion. They know each other well from the business community. Hans van der Jagt introduces his wife.

lines.speaker: Raymond van Dieren
lines.dutch: Goedenavond Hans.
lines.pronunciation: khoo-dern-aa-font hans
lines.translation: Good evening, Hans.

lines.speaker: Hans van der Jagt
lines.dutch: Goedenavond Raymond, hoe gaat het! Mag ik je mijn vrouw Rita voorstellen?
lines.pronunciation: khoo-dern-aa-font ray-mont hoo khaat het. mahk ik yer mayn frow ree-taa foar-steh-lern
lines.translation: Good evening Raymond, how are you? May I introduce my wife Rita to you?

lines.speaker: Raymond van Dieren
lines.dutch: Goedenavond mevrouw Van der Jagt, ik ben Raymond van Dieren van Biz Accountants. Prettig met u kennis te maken!
lines.pronunciation: khoo-dern-aa-font mer-frow fan der yahkt. ik ben ray-mont fan diee-rem fan biz er-kown-terns. preh-tikh met uw keh-nis ter maa-kern
lines.translation: Good evening Mrs Van der Jagt, I am Raymond van Dieren of Biz Accountants. Nice to meet you!

lines.speaker: Rita van der Jagt
lines.dutch: Insgelijks. Hans heeft mij al veel over u verteld. Woon t u nog steeds in Amsterdam- Noord?
lines.pronunciation: ins-kher-layks. hans hayft may al fayl oa-fer uw fer-telt. voant uw nokh stayts in am-ster-dam-noart
lines.translation: Likewise. My husband has told me a lot about you. Do you still live in the northern part of Amsterdam?

lines.speaker: Raymond van Dieren
lines.dutch: Nee, ik woon nu op het Java-eiland.
lines.pronunciation: nay ik voan nuw op jaa-faa-ay-lant
lines.translation: No, I am now living on the Java-eiland.

text: Saying Goodbye

When it's time to say goodbye, you can say (both formal and informal) Tot ziens (tot zeens) or Dag! (dakh) or (very informal) Doei! (dooy), or Doeg! (doohkh). If it was an informal meeting with friends, you say Het was gezellig (het vas kher-zeh-likh) (We had a nice time). If people have been speaking about their plans or working on something, you often end with a wish: Veel succes! (fayl suwk-ses) (Good luck!).

In business, when leaving, you generally mention things to be done, like Ik stuur u zo spoedig mogelijk het voorstel (ik stuur uw zoa snel moa-kher-lerk het foar-stel) (I'll send you our proposal as soon as possible) or Ik wacht uw verslag af (ik vakht uw fer-slakkh af) (I'll wait for your report).
Talkin' the Talk
Cilla Vermeent and Gerda Jongsma have met at Mike Johnson's party in Laren. They say goodbye.

lines.speaker: Gerda
lines.dutch: Het is al laat, ik moet naar huis. Het was leuk om je te leren kennen.
lines.pronunciation: het is al laat ik moot naar hoais. het vas luk om yer ter lay-rern keh-nern
lines.translation: It is late, I have to go home now. It was nice meeting you.

lines.speaker: Cilla
lines.dutch: Ja, het was gezellig. Veel succes met je plannen.
lines.pronunciation: yaa het vas kher-zeh-likh. fayl suwk-ses met yer pla-nern
lines.translation: Yes, we had a nice time. Lots of luck with your plans.

lines.speaker: Gerda
lines.dutch: Bedankt en tot ziens.
lines.pronunciation: ber-dankt en tot zeens
lines.translation: Thanks, bye.

text: Chatting about Towns, Countries, and Languages
Introducing is a good start, but how to start a conversation? In this section you learn how to say where you are from, how to ask from where the other person is and which languages he or she speaks.
Telling where you are from
All you need are the words: Ik kom uit . . . (ik kom oait) (I am from ...).

When saying this, most people refer to the place where they are living at that moment. This is seldom the place where they were born. When people think it is important to mention their birthplace, they say: Ik kom uit Amsterdam, maar ik ben geboren op Curaçao. (ik kom oait am-ster-dam maar ik ben kher-boa-rem op kuw-raa-sow) (I am from Amsterdam, but I was born on the island Curaçao). Normally they stick to: Ik kom uit. Using this expression, you can refer to a village, town, region or country. Here are some examples:
Do you know the following European capitals and countries? Table 4-1 shows you how to pronounce them.
To be: the verb 'zijn'

One of the most important verbs in all languages is to be. In Dutch zijn (zayn). Just like in English this verb is used in order to describe something: from moods as in verdrietig zijn (fer-dree-tikh zayn) (to be sad) or blij zijn (blay zayn) (to be happy) to physical characteristics like groot zijn (khroot zayn) (to be tall) and slank zijn (slank zayn) (to be slim). Zijn is a very irregular verb.
Asking Where Somebody Is From

When you want to ask a person where they are from, you first have to decide if you want to be formal or informal with them. If you want to be informal you have to make a choice between singular (if you address one person) or plural (if you address two or more persons). So you choose one of these three:
Talkin' the Talk
Sytske and Kirstin meet each other on a canal trip in Amsterdam.

lines.speaker: Kirstin
lines.dutch: Waar kom jij vandaan?
lines.pronunciation: vaar kom yay fan-daan
lines.translation: Where are you from?

lines.speaker: Sytske
lines.dutch: Uit Sneek, dat is in Friesland
lines.pronunciation: oait snayk dat is in fees-lant
lines.translation: From Sneek, that is in Friesland

lines.speaker: Kirstin
lines.dutch: Waar ligt Friesland?
lines.pronunciation: vaar likht fees-lant
lines.translation: Where is Friesland?

lines.speaker: Sytske
lines.dutch: In het noorden van Nederland. En waar kom jij vanda- aan?
lines.pronunciation: in het noar-dern fan nay-der-lant. en vaar kom yay fan-daan
lines.translation: In the north of the Netherlands. And where are you from?

lines.speaker: Kirstin
lines.dutch: Ik kom uit Duitsland. Ik kom uit Berlijn.
lines.pronunciation: ik kom oait doaits-lant. ik kom oait behr-layn
lines.translation: I am from Germany. I am from Berlin.

text: To come: komen
You'll meet this Dutch verb often. It is a regular verb.
Learning Something about Nationalities
While chatting about the country where you are from, the person you are talking to might ask you which nationality you are and which is your own language.
In Table 4-2 you'll find several countries, the right words to tell your nationality as well as the Dutch words for the languages that are spoken in those countries.

caption: Country Names, Male and Female Nouns, and Adjectives

text: Using these terms in a sentence

phrases.translation: Cilla Vermeent is from the Netherlands.

phrases.dutch: Mike Johnson komt uit de Verenigde Staten.
phrases.pronunciation: mike john-son komt oait der fer-ray-nikh-ter staa-tern
phrases.translation: Mike Johnson is from the US.

text: Chatting about languages
You use the verb spreken (to speak) in order to chat about languages.
Talkin' the Talk
Kirstin and Sytske are on a canal tour in Amsterdam. The guide speaks English, German, and Spanish. Kirstin notices that Sytske understands Spanish.

lines.speaker: Kirstin
lines.dutch: Spreek je ook Spaans?
lines.pronunciation: sprayk yer oak spaans
lines.translation: Do you speak Spanish as well?

lines.speaker: Sytske
lines.dutch: Ja, ik spreek Spaans. En jij?
lines.pronunciation: yaa, ik sprayk spaans. en yay
lines.translation: Yes, I do speak Spanish. And you?

lines.speaker: Kirstin
lines.dutch: Nee, ik spreek alleen Duits en een beetje Nederlands. Spreek jij Duits?
lines.pronunciation: nay ik sprayk a-layn doaits en een bay-tie-ies nay-der-lants. sprayk yay doaits
lines.translation: No, I just speak German and some Dutch. Do you speak German?

lines.speaker: Sytske
lines.dutch: Nee, ik spreek geen Duits. Ik spreek Fries, Nederlands, Engels en Spaans.
lines.pronunciation: nay ik sprayk khayn doaits. ik sprayk fees nay-der-lants eng-erts en spaans
lines.translation: No, I don't speak German. I speak Frisian, Dutch, English and Spanish.

lines.speaker: Kirstin
lines.dutch: Spreken alle Nederlanders zoveel talen?
lines.pronunciation: spray-kern a-ler nay-der-lan-ders zoa-fayl taa-lern
lines.translation: Do all Dutch people speak so many languages?

lines.speaker: Sytske
lines.dutch: Alle Nederlanders leren op school Nederlands en nog twee talen. Alleen Friezen spreken Fries.
lines.pronunciation: a-ler nay-der-lan-ders lay-rem op skhoal nay-der-lans en nokh tvay taa-lern. A-layn free-zern spray-kern frees
lines.translation: All Dutch learn Dutch and two more languages at school. Only Frisians speak Frisian.

text: Getting to Know Each Other Better
In This Chapter

If you really want to know somebody you have to talk with him. Using the social talk of this chapter, you will not only make new contacts, but also learn to talk Dutch. Whether you are talking on the tram or on a bus, on a plane or at a party: there are always things you can talk about. Ask questions, talk about yourself or about the weather.

When people really get interested in you, they might ask questions about your family. You will find useful words for family talk in the last but one part of this chapter. In case you want to stick to more neutral subjects, a chat about the weather will help you to break the ice.
Inviting the Other to Talk

Do you find it difficult to make contact? Use questions for an opening. Ask people whether they know the place where you are going to or where you are. They will answer you and if they are interested in you, they will ask you a question in return. At a later stage you can ask more personal questions. The following opening sentences might be useful:

phrases.dutch: Bent u hier voor de eerste keer?
phrases.pronunciation: bent uw heer foar der ayr-ster kayr
phrases.translation: Is this the first time you're here? (formal)

phrases.dutch: Ben je hier voor de eerste keer?
phrases.pronunciation: ben yer heer foar der ayr-ster kayr
phrases.translation: Is this the first time you're here? (informal)
Are we going to arrive soon?
Will we have to wait a long time?

text: All questions that start with a verb are 'closed questions'. The person you're talking to might answer them with a simple 'yes' or 'no'.

Open questions start with a question word. Question words are words such as wie (wee) (who?), wat (vat) (what?), waar (vaar) (where?), hoe (hoo) (how?) and wanneer (vaa-nayr) (when?). If you ask an open question the person you're talking to will give a longer answer than only ja (yaa) (yes) or nee (nay) (no). Here are some suitable open questions that start with a question word:

phrases.dutch: Wat is dit voor soort restaurant?
phrases.pronunciation: vat is dit foar soart res-to-rant
phrases.translation: What kind of restaurant is this?

text: When you are at a party, you can ask the other person about his relationship with the host:

dutch: Hoe lang kent u de familie Sturney al?
pronunciation: hoo lang kent uw der faa-mee-lee stürr-may al
translation: How long have you known the Sturney family?

text: People will talk longer when you ask them questions that also require a personal statement. See what happens when you ask one of the following questions:

translation: Do you know Alan Sturney well?

text: See for more information about questions the section on asking questions Chapter 2.
Talking about Yourself

When you talk about yourself, tell the person you are speaking to the things you would like to know about him or her! You may say what kind of work you do and where you are from. Perhaps at the end of the conversation you want to give them your telephone number.
Talking about your work
Generally you can tell what kind of work you do, using the words 'I am' in combination with your profession or function. You don't use an article. Some professions have masculine and feminine forms.

A lot of professions once had a feminine form and have now lost that. In this case, you always use the masculine form. Women generally say Ik ben directeur (ik ben di-rek-turr) (I am a director) instead of the old-fashioned Ik ben directrice (ik ben di-rek-tree-ser) (I am a director). Young teachers will say Ik ben docent Nederlands. (ik ben doa-sent nay-der-lans) (I am a teacher of Dutch) Only elderly women still use the feminine form Ik ben docente Nederlands. (ik ben doa-sen-ter nay-der-lans) (I am a teacher of Dutch).
More and more professions have English names. You'll find the next professions among your Dutch business partners:

phrases.translation: I am a human resource assistant.

text: If you don't find the word for your profession, check the dictionary or a dictionary on the Internet. You can also opt for another possibility and mention the place where you work:

phrases.dutch: Ik werk bij een internationaal bedrijf.
phrases.pronunciation: ik verk bay ern in-ter-nashoa-naal ber-drayf
phrases.translation: I work in an international company.

text: When you're a student, you may want to mention what you study. Just start saying: Ik studeer (ik stuw-dayr) (I study) and then add:
In case you're doing something else, the following sentences might come in handy:

phrases.dutch: Ik ben hier op tijdelijke basis.
phrases.pronunciation: ik ben heer op tay-der-le-ker baa-sis

text: Asking and giving a telephone number

When you first offer to give your telephone number, the other person will probably give his telephone number in return. So if you're interested in staying in touch, you might say: Ik geef je mijn telefoonnummer in geval je contact met me wilt opnemen (ik khayf yer mayn tay-ler-foa-nurr-mer in kher-fal dat yer contakt met merr vil op-nay-mern) (I'll give you my telephone number in case you want to get in touch with me). Generally you'll write down your number or you'll give your business card. After handling over the card, you can add: Dit is mijn mobiele nummer (dit is mern moa-bee-lee nurr-mer) (This is my mobile number), or het netnummer is .. (het net-nummer is) (the dialing/area code is .. ) , en het abonneenummer is .. ( het a-bo-nayn-murr is ..) (the subscriber's number is...). A good sentence to end the exchange of telephone numbers is: Je kunt me altijd bellen (yer kunt mer al-tayt beh-lern) (You can always call me).

Dutch telephone numbers always have ten digits. The first two, three or four digits stand for the dialing/area code: 06 for cell phones, 0 plus two digits for the major cities, and 0 plus three digits for the smaller towns.
In the phone book the subscriber's number starts with three digits and then is divided in groups of two.
020-679 04 28: nul twintig, zes zeven negen, nul vier, twee acht (nuhl twin-tikh, zes zay-vern nay-khern, nuhl feer, tway akht) (zero twenty, zero seven nine, zero four, two eight)

In Web sites, on business cards and on official papers you'll find telephone numbers divided like this. When you ask a private person for his telephone number, he will give it the way it sounds best to him: very often in separate figures, but other combinations are also possible. You can even hear partners mentioning their common telephone number in different ways! One partner will say:
036-532 532 1: nul zesendertig, vijf drie twee, vijf drie twee, één (nuhl zessern-dehrtikh, fayf dree tway, fayf dree tway, ayn) (zero thirty six, five three two, five three two, one)
The other partner will tell you:

036-53 25 321: nul zesendertig, drieënvijftig, vijfentwintig, drie twee één (nuhl zessern-dehrtikh, dree-ern-fayf-terkh, fayf-ern-twin-terkh, dree tway ayn) (zero thirty-six, fifty-three, twenty-five, three two one)

Cold comfort: Dutch people generally agree about the dialling code: It always starts with zero and the tens are pronounced as tens, so nul tien (nuhl teen) (zero ten) and nul twintig (nuhl twin-terkh) (zero twenty). In case the dialling code has four figures, is is pronounced as 0320 nul drie twee nul (nuhl dree tway nuhl), like separate figures.
Talkin' the Talk
Cilla Vermeent is at a party. She is having her first glass of wine when she meets Mike Johnson. She immediately notices that he is not a Dutchman, though he speaks Dutch rather well.

lines.speaker: Cilla Vermeent
lines.dutch: Wat heeft u naar Nederland gebracht?
lines.pronunciation: vat hayft uw naar nay-der-lant kher-brakht
lines.translation: What brought you to the Netherlands?

lines.speaker: Mike Johnson
lines.dutch: Ik ben hier op tijdelijke basis. Ik werk voor een internationaal bedrijf.
lines.pronunciation: ik ben heer op tay-der-le-ker baa-sis. ik verk foor ern in-ter-naa-shoa-naal ber-drayf
lines.translation: I am here temporarily. I work for an international company.

lines.speaker: Cilla Vermeent
lines.dutch: En welk bedrijf is dat, als ik het vragen mag?
lines.pronunciation: en welk ber-drayf is dat, als ik fraa-khern makh
lines.translation: And which company is that, if I may ask?

lines.speaker: Mike Johnson
lines.dutch: Ik werk voor Golfwagen Duitsland en ben nu in Amsterdam gestationeerd.
lines.pronunciation: ik verk foor kholt-vaa-khern doaits-lant en ben nuw in am-ster-dam kher-staa-sho-nayrt
lines.translation: I'm with Golfwagen Germany and I'm now stationed in Amsterdam.

lines.speaker: Cilla Vermeent
lines.dutch: Bent u dan Duits?
lines.pronunciation: bent uw dan doaits
lines.translation: In that case, are you German?

lines.speaker: Mike Johnson
lines.dutch: Mijn moeder is Duits en mijn vader is Amerikaans.
lines.pronunciation: mayn moo-der is doaits en en mayn faa-der is a-may-ree-kaans
lines.translation: My mother is German and my father is American.

lines.speaker: Cilla Vermeent
lines.dutch: Waar woont u?
lines.pronunciation: vaar woont uw
lines.translation: Where do you live?

lines.speaker: Mike Johnson
lines.dutch: Doordeweeks woon ik in een hotel in Naarden. In het weekend ga ik naar Keulen, naar mijn vrouw. Dat is maar een paar uur rijden. En waar woon jij?
lines.pronunciation: doar-der-vayks voan ik in ern hoa-tel in naar-dern. in het vee-kent khaa ik naar ku-lern naar mayn frow. het is maar ern paar uwr ray-dern. en vaar voan yay
lines.translation: During the week, I live in a hotel in Naarden. In the weekends I go to Cologne, to my wife. It's only a couple of hours' driving. Where do you live?

lines.speaker: Cilla Vermeent
lines.dutch: Hier vlakbij, in Kortenhoef. Blijft u vanavond in Nederland?
lines.pronunciation: heer vlak-bay in kor-tern-hoef. blayft uw faa-naa-font in nay-der-lant
lines.translation: Nearby, in Kortenhoef. Are you staying in the Netherlands tonight?

lines.speaker: Mike Johnson
lines.dutch: Nee, ik rijd straks naar huis.
lines.pronunciation: nay ik rays straks naar hoais
lines.translation: No, I will drive home soon.

lines.speaker: Cilla Vermeent
lines.dutch: O, dus daarom drinkt u geen alcohol. Ik wens u een goeie reis!
lines.pronunciation: oa, duhs daa-rom drinkt uw kheen al-koa-hol. ik wens u ern khaa-yer rays
lines.translation: So that's why you don't drink alcohol. I wish you a good trip!

text: Telling about your family

When you are getting to know each other better you may talk about your family. In non-business circumstances, women talk to other women about their children. This is very natural after work and when you're in child-friendly surroundings, such as schools, sports fields and swimming pools. Be careful in businesslike situations: Dutch bosses want you to stick to your work when you're working! Talking about your family is something you do when you get confidential with people or when they ask questions about it. You can use the following words:

Divorce is almost as popular as family life in the Netherlands. In the larger cities you'll meet a lot of alleenstaanden (a-layer-staan-dern) (singles). Some of them stay single, others have relationships but keep away from marriage.

Dutch has many words for the people you are related to. A man who mentions mijn vriend Marcel (mayn freent mar-sel), probably met Marcel at school or when studying. They have kept in touch. Whenever a woman talks about mijn vriend (mayn freent) (without mentioning the name) she is probably refers to her partner in life. When she mentions mijn vriendin Gerda (mayn freen-din kherr-daa), she probably refers to a school or study friend with whom she kept in touch. Conversely, when a man talks about mijn vriendin (mayn freen-din), he is probably referring to his life partner.
As the words mijn vriend and mijn vriendin may cause confusion it's safer to use mijn partner (mayn part-ner) when talking about your life partner.

A married man says mijn vrouw (mayn frow) when referring to his wife. Elderly men or younger men who want to indicate a certain distance to their partner call her mijn echtgenote (mayn ekht-kher-noa-ter) (my spouse). A

married woman says mijn man (mayn man) when referring to her husband. Elderly women or younger women who want to indicate a certain distance to their partner refer to her him as mijn echtgenoot (mayn ekht-kher-noat).
Talkin' the Talk

Cilla has met Gabriele Neuland from München at the election ceremony of Secretary of the Year in Amsterdam. Gabriele is an executive secretary working with Golfwagen in Amsterdam. When Cilla and Gabriele meet for the second time they talk about their families.

lines.speaker: Cilla
lines.dutch: Heb je broers en zussen?
lines.pronunciation: hep yer broors en zuh-sern
lines.translation: Have you got any brothers and sisters?

lines.speaker: Gabriele
lines.dutch: Ik heb één zus in Duitsland.
lines.pronunciation: ik hep ayn zuhs in doaits-lant
lines.translation: I've got one sister in Germany.

lines.speaker: Cilla
lines.dutch: Wat toevallig, ik heb ook één zus.
lines.pronunciation: vat too-fa-likh ik hep oak ayn zuhs
lines.translation: What a coincidence, I have one sister as well!

lines.speaker: Gabriele
lines.dutch: Is ze ouder of jonger dan jij?
lines.pronunciation: is zer ow-der of yong-er dan yay
lines.translation: Is she older or younger than you are?

lines.speaker: Cilla
lines.dutch: Ze is ouder. En die van jou?
lines.pronunciation: zer is ow-der. en dee fan yow
lines.translation: She's older. And yours?

lines.speaker: Gabriele
lines.dutch: De mijne ook, wat toevallig!
lines.pronunciation: der may-ner oak vat too-fa-likh
lines.translation: Mine is older as well, what a coincidence!

lines.speaker: Cilla
lines.dutch: Heeft jouw zus kinderen?
lines.pronunciation: hayft yow zuhs oak kin-der-ern
lines.translation: Has your sister got any children?

lines.speaker: Gabriele
lines.dutch: Ja, twee: een jongen en een meisje.
lines.pronunciation: ya tway ern yong-ern en ern may-sher
lines.translation: Yes, two, a boy and a girl.

lines.speaker: Cilla
lines.dutch: Nou, dan hebben we nu een verschil gevonden: mijn zus is niet getrouwd en heeft geen kinderen.
lines.pronunciation: now dan heb-bern ver nuw ern fer-skihil kher-fon-dern mayn zuhs is neet kher-trowt en hayft khayn kin-der-ern
lines.translation: Well then, we've found a difference now: my sister is not married and has no children.

text: Negating: 'niet' and 'geen'
Dutch has two ways of negating. The first is by combining niet (neet) with a verb.
The second is by combining geen with a noun: either a person or a thing.
Between geen (khayn) and the person or thing you may place an adjective that tells something about the person or thing.

phrases.dutch: Mijn zus heeft geen kleine kinderen.
phrases.pronunciation: mayn zu-ster hayft khayn klay-nerr kin-der-ern
phrases.translation: My sister has no small children.

text: Dealing with your neighbours. The Dutch spend a lot of time in and around the house, especially in winter. Their house is their castle, and generally they don't like people to drop in uninvited unless they're very good friends. When they ask you Kom eens langs (kom aynslangs) (Drop by one day) you should respond: Wanneer komt dat uit? (vaa-nayr komt dat oat) (What is convenient for you?). They will have a look in their diary or first have to check with their partner. Then they will tell you when: in the morning or in the evening, for coffee, before dinner or just for a drink. If you are very familiar with your neighbours and sometimes just walk in, don't do that during dinner time, which is between 6 and 7 p.m. Your neighbours will feel embarrassed. Similarly, your neighbours will avoid visiting you while you are having dinner.
Talking about the Weather

The Dutch like to talk about the weather. Even when you work and live in a town, the weather is important: what are you going to wear, what are you going to do, are you going to walk, cycle, or take the bus to work, and even how moody will your colleagues be today? Talking about the weather is a favourite pastime among the Dutch. Here are some phrases to join them:
How's the weather?
Start your sentence with het is (het is) (It is):

Note that Dutchmen start their chat about the weather mentioning things that the person with whom they're talking will probably have noticed too. In order to share your feelings about the weather (happiness, disappointment or anger) you can add the word hè (heh) and then make your sentence a question by raising the tone at the end of the sentence. For instance, Het is koud hè? (het is kout heh) (It's cold, isn't it?) or Het is heet hè? (het is hayt heh) (It's hot, isn't it?). This remark in the form of a question will cause a reaction, probably something like: Ik moest krabben (ik moost kra-bem)
(I had to scrape the ice off my car windows) or ja, hadden we maar airco (yaa haa-dern ver maar ayr-co) (Yes, I wish we had air conditioning).
As Dutch weather can be very changeable, the following weather descriptions will come in handy:
Watching the weather forecast on TV, you might hear some of the next sentences:

phrases.dutch: 's Ochtends is er kans op mist.
phrases.pronunciation: sokh-terns is ehr kans op mist
phrases.translation: In the morning it might be foggy.

phrases.dutch: 's Ochtends is er kans op gladheid.
phrases.pronunciation: sokh-terns is ehr kans op khlaht-hayt
phrases.translation: In the morning it might be slippery.

text: Talking about the temperature
When the person you talk to about the weather has said something in reaction to your remark, you might confirm your shared observations by adding some detail, like the temperature, saying:

phrases.pronunciation: het is teen khraa-dern on-der nuhl

phrases.dutch: Het is 30 graden in de schaduw.
phrases.pronunciation: het is dherr-tikh khraa-dern in der skhaa-duw
phrases.translation: It's thirty degrees in the shade.

text: And finish the chat saying:

translation: Tomorrow it will be even colder.

text: or:

translation: Tomorrow it will be even hotter.

text: Talkin' the Talk

Gerda and Jessica are members of the same gym. In summer they do some open-air sports as well, such as biking or running. They have agreed on running on Saturday morning, 10 o'clock. They meet in the gym.

lines.speaker: Gerda
lines.dutch: Hallo Jessica, hoe gaat het?
lines.pronunciation: ha-loa yay-see-kaa hoo khaat het

text: Enjoying a Meal and Eating Out
In This Chapter

items: Entering a restaurant and sitting down
Shopping for food at the traditional market

text: Food, eating habits, and eating out are some of the best ways to get to know a country. Whether you are cooking yourself and having dinner with friends or having a business lunch: it's always useful to know how to talk about food.
Enjoy Your Meal

Eating out in the Netherlands is an international experience. Especially in the western part of the Netherlands it's difficult to find restaurants with 'typical' Dutch food; it's easier to find restaurants with non-Dutch food!

Until some 30 years ago the traditional Dutch meal consisted of (boiled) potatoes, vegetables and meat. After 1950, when many people came back from the former Dutch Indies, 'Chinese food' became popular for eating out. It was not actually food from China, but the food Chinese people prepared in the Indies for their masters: spicy and sweet-and-sour. After 1960, Italian food entered the Dutch kitchen. It was mostly considered fast food. Travelling abroad became more and more popular and so did food that people got to know on

their holidays, such as Spanish and Greek. This process went on in the 1970s and 1980s. Hamburger chains introduced fast food, and in the 1990s supermarkets started to sell fast food too. As a counterbalance to all this high-calorie food the 'nouvelle cuisine' became popular in the more expensive restaurants: refined international food. You can recognise this kind of restaurant by the carefully set tables with lots of wine glasses and white tablecloths.

The big cities offer a large variety of restaurants to choose from, from virtually every country. Of course, you'll also find these elsewhere in Europe, except for the Chinese-Indonesian ones from the former Dutch Indies. You'll recognise the Chinese-Indonesian restaurants by their traditional look: generally they are decorated with red and gold or green and gold. Try one of them! As an exception to most other restaurants, they also serve hot lunches, and their service is quick.

For expensive business lunches and dinners 'nouvelle cuisine' is still popular. Ask your colleagues for the names of good restaurants! In the bookshops near stations, you'll find all kinds of restaurant guides.
Is it time to eat?

Traditionally, the Dutch had three meals: breakfast, lunch and dinner. Breakfast is losing its popularity in many Dutch homes, but hotels will serve it in the morning in between 7 and 10. The hotel breakfast is generally international. It has juice, cereals, milk products, bread, butter, marmalade, cheese, sliced cold meat, and fruit.

Dutch breakfast at home is modest: a glass of juice, a cup of tea or coffee, maybe some cereals. The traditional slice of bread with cheese, marmalade or chocoladehagel (shoa-koo-laa-der-haa-khert) (chocolate sprinkling) is disappearing. In the western part of Holland many commuters take their breakfast in their car while in the traffic jam: a breakfast drink or some coffee from home and a wrapped snack or candy bar. Train stations offer breakfast drinks, hot coffee, and snacks.

Lunch is somewhere between 12 o'clock and 12.30. If you are from the southern part of Europe, you will be disappointed! Dutch lunch is plain: some bread rolls with ham or cheese and a glass of milk. People often bring their own lunch from home: a sandwich or some fruit. Having lunch takes them just 10 minutes. As the law obliges employers to organise a one-hour lunch break, people spend the rest of the time on their mobiles, browsing the Internet or going out for a walk.

Lunches are more elaborate when taken in a restaurants. Restaurants offer something warm in combination with bread rolls: soup, a slice of pizza or a kroket (croquette). As nowadays only farmers and shift workers have their
main meal at noon, a business lunch, even when it is taken in a starred restaurant, will always be a light meal.

Dinner is the main meal. You have it somewhere between 6 and 8 at home or between 7 and 10 o'clock in a restaurant. The dinner at home can be anything. A small group of Dutch people stick to their traditional potatoes, meat, and vegetables. Processed food and fast food are becoming popular. The supermarkets offer a wide range of prepared food that can be heated in the oven or microwave. At home dinner consists of a main dish and some dessert. The dessert may be fruit, but it generally is one of the hundreds of dairy products offered in supermarkets, such as vla (custard).

In restaurants, three dishes are offered: a first course, a main course, and dessert. Coffee or tea are served as well, or you go to some other place to have them there. Many people, especially women, skip one of the dishes, either first course or dessert. They wait for the others to finish their course – the main course is eaten by all guests at the same time.
Setting the Table
When you're eating in a restaurant you'll find on your table the following items:
When something is missing on the table, you can ask the waiter:

phrases.translation: May I have a spoon, please?

text: When eating at home you might use the same items for setting the table in the traditional way, either with een tafellaken (een taa-fer-laa-kem) (a table-cloth) or with placemats (plays-mats) (place-mats). Or you can join most young Dutch people and have dinner seated on de bank (der bank) (the couch) while watching TV.
Using more of them: plurals

You can divide the plurals of Dutch nouns (nouns are words that can be preceded by de, het or een) in two main groups. The biggest group has a plural ending in -en: de borden (der bor-dern) (the plates), de vorken (der for-kern) (the forks).
The second group has a plural ending in -s, such as de lepels (der lay-perls) (the spoons), de kopjes (der kop-yers) (the cups).

How can you know whether the plural suffix is -en or -s? Words that end in -el, -en, -er, -em, -erd, -e, -je or -aar, get an -s. It may be difficult to remember this long row, but there is some logic to it: all the mentioned suffixes of these words are unstressed. So words that end in an unstressed syllable, often get -s.

Almost all diminutives (words that are used to indicate small things or small persons) end in an unstressed -je or -tje, such as het kopje (het kop-yer) (the little cup) en het lepeltje (het lay-perl-tyer) (the little spoon). Following the general rules for
plurals they get an -s: de kopjes (der kop-yers) (the little cups) en de lepeltjes (der lay-perl-tyers) (the little spoons).
The second, far bigger, group consists of words that do not end in an unstressed -el, -en, -er, -em, -erd, -e, -je or -aar. They get -en for the plural.

So far so good. When you are speaking, you won't have too many difficulties with the plurals, because you won't have time to think of the rules. Very often you will just imitate other people. After some time, you will know most plurals by intuition. However, when you start writing, there are complications in the spelling of the words.
It's beyond the reach of this book to treat them all, but here are some examples:
In each of these words a doubling occurs of the consonant at the end of the first syllable, in order to keep the vowel sound short. Consonants are all letters that are not a, e, i, o, or u.
In other cases you'll have to employ a trick in order write the long vowels (a, e, i, o and u) correctly. Compare the spelling of the singulars with that of the plurals:
For more information about short and long vowels see Chapter 1.

Most important changes in the spelling of the consonants take place in words that end in -f or -s. The singular de brief (der breef) (the letter) is written as de brieven (der bree-vem) in plural. The singular het huis (het hoais) (the house) becomes de huizen (der hoai-zem).
You are ready to use more of them now!
Essential Verbs at the Table
Drinken (drin-kern) (to drink) and eten (ay-tem) (to eat) are essential to stay alive and so it's important to be able to use them when you're living in the Netherlands.
To drink: the verb 'drinken'

The verb drinken is regular. Take off the -en and you have the first person. For the second (you informal) and the third (he, she and you formal) person just add -t. For the plurals (we, you plural informal and they) you can take the whole verb or infinitive: drinken.
To eat: the verb 'eten'

The verb eten (ay-tem) is regular as well. However, it has some complications when spelling it. In order to make the e (ay) sound like a long vowel you have to double it in the first, second and third person. (I, you, he, she, and you formal).
At the Restaurant

Eating out is popular for singles and couples. A lot of Dutch people consider eating out a luxury – people go to restaurants on holidays such as Boxing Day or when they have something to celebrate. Families with young children will visit hamburger chains and pancake houses on family outings. Grill restaurants are popular when the children grow older.
Choosing your restaurant
Big towns have a large choice of restaurants. An Argentijns grillrestaurant (ar-khern-tayns khri-res-to-rant) (an Argentinian grill restaurant) offers you large and low-priced meat dishes.

In seaport towns such as Amsterdam and Rotterdam you may find a genuine Chinees restaurant (shee-nays res-to-rant) (a Chinese restaurant). The food in Chinese restaurants is very different from the Chinese-Indonesian restaurants. Dutch people erroneously call the traditional Chinese-Indonesian restaurants de Chinees (der shee-nays) (The Chinese). Chinese food from China is not spicy and not sweet and sour like the Chinese-Indonesian from the former Dutch East Indies colony, the present Indonesia.

phrases.translation: to have Chinese-Indonesian food has always been popular among those who want large meals for a reasonable price
to go to a French restaurant. It is possible in the big towns. Franse restaurants (fran-ser res-to-rants) (restaurants offering French cuisine) generally are exclusive and expensive
Indian food restaurants, in the larger towns
Dutch restaurants, hardly exist and are very difficult to find. Only a few restaurants specialise in traditional Dutch food such as pancakes and peasoup, mostly for the tourists
to have Thai/Vietnamese food. It is possible in a lot of restaurants in the big towns
fish restaurants, can be found in larger towns and those with a harbour
to have international food, in the categories Cajun or fusion, Greek, Italian, Mexican, Spanish, and so on. It is possible in almost every town

phrases.dutch: Als u een vegetarisch restaurant zoekt
phrases.translation: vegetarian restaurant, buy a good guide in a bookshop or look at www.ivens.nl

Business restaurants with three or more stars, are generally expensive and not necessarily in the city centre. You can find them in special guides or by recommendation of your colleagues. You generally go to them by car and they have good parking facilities

text: Places for lunch
Dutch lunches are plain and generally not hot.

phrases.dutch: Als u niet al te hongerig bent, probeer dan een haringkraam
phrases.translation: a seafood car, voor een haring (haa-ring) (herring) of een lekkerbekje (em leh-ker-beh-kyer) (deep-fried fish fillet)

phrases.translation: a fries/chips stall, voor een patatje (pa-tat-yer) (portion of fries/chips) of frikadel (free-ka-del) (minced-meat hotdog)

phrases.dutch: Als u iets gezonds wilt, ga dan voor een broodje gezond
phrases.translation: a CLT roll with cheese, egg, tomato, and some lettuce or cucumber, in een croissanterie (kra-san-ter-ree) (a croissant shop) of een broodjeszaak (em broyt-yers-zaak) (a sandwich bar)

a snack bar, of een cafetaria (ka-feh-taa-ree-aa) (a cafeteria), kunt u veel van de hierboven genoemde dingen krijgen, plus soep of een uitsmijter (oyt-smay-ter) (fried eggs and ham on two slices of bread)

phrases.dutch: In sommige steden vindt u een poffertjeskraam
phrases.translation: These traditional tiny pancakes are eaten with sugar and butter. Children like them very much

a pancake, in een pannenkoekenhuis (paa-ner-koo-ken-hoais) (pancake house) is a substantial lunch, especially when you take the traditional spekpannenkoek (spek-paa-ner-kook). This pancake is a curious mix of sweet and salty: it has a lot of bacon on it and is eaten with syrup

text: At the end of the afternoon, you may long for an alcoholic beverage and something salty. If you want to go international, find a tapas bar and accompany a glass of wine with small portions of olives, fish, or meat.

In case you are looking for something really Dutch, enter a bruin café (em broain kaa-fay) (a 'brown café' or pub) and have een biertje (em beer-tyer) (a beer) or een borrel (em bo-rel) (a drink). In the traditional brown café, snacks are limited to een portie kaas (em por-see kaas) (a portion of cheese) or een portie leverworst (em por-see lay-ver-vorst) (a portion of liver sausage).

In a café (ka-fay) (a café, pub, or bar) alcohol is the main thing you will find. Some cafés serve een portie saté (em por-see saa-tay) (a portion of satay), pieces of pork meat on a stick, served with a warm, spicy peanut sauce, or perhaps een portie bitterballen (em por-see bit-ter-bah-lern) (a type of croquette, served as an appetiser). There are many different kinds of cafés, mostly with their own group of clients, but they will not be as old and brown as the bruin café.

Eating herring. The older generation loves herring. Though many young people are horrified by the thought of eating raw fish, the salty herring, garnished with onions, is offered as an exquisite bite at parties and receptions. Especially, the first young herring of the season, nieuwe haring (nee-wer haa-ring) (new herring), sold in May, is exquisite and expensive. However, in the big towns and on traditional markets fish shops sell this Dutch speciality to those who love it. Try one when you have drunk a lot of beer the night before. They say herring is a cure for hangovers!

When you're really hungry, long for a beer or glass of wine and you don't want to spend too much on food, try an eetcafé (erm ayht-ka-fay) (bar/pub serving meals). The owners will serve you simple food in a relaxed ambiance.
Coffeeshops (ko-fee-shops) (coffee shops) are places to buy and enjoy marihuana legally. See a guide for a selection!
Making a reservation

For some restaurants you can make a reservation on the Internet. You can also call after three in the afternoon and make a reservation for the night or for the weekend. Make sure to put in a reservation for trendy and business restaurants! The following sentences will be helpful:

phrases.dutch: Ik wil graag een tafel reserveren.
phrases.pronunciation: ik vil khraakh em taa-ferl ray-ser-vay-rem
phrases.translation: I would like to reserve a table.

phrases.dutch: Ik wil een tafel reserveren voor vier personen om zeven uur. Is dat mogelijk?
phrases.pronunciation: ik vil em taa-ferl ray-ser-vay-rem foor feer persoa-nem om zay-fern uwr. is dat mog-kher-letk
phrases.translation: I would like to reserve a table for four at 7 p.m. Is that possible?

text: In order to be specific, you have to mention the time and day. For example:
The following complete sentences might come in handy:

phrases.dutch: Ik wil graag een tafel voor vanavond reserveren.
phrases.pronunciation: ik vil khraakh em taa-ferl foor fa-naa-font ray-ser-vay-rem
phrases.translation: I would like to reserve a table for tonight.

phrases.dutch: Heeft u een vrije tafel voor morgenavond om zeven uur?

text: Entering a Restaurant and Sitting Down
If you go into a restaurant without a reservation, the following sentences might be useful:

phrases.dutch: Heeft u plaats voor twee personen?
phrases.pronunciation: hayft uw plaats foor tvay persoa-nern
phrases.translation: Have you got place for two persons?

phrases.dutch: Nee, het spijt me, we zijn volgeboekt voor vanavond.
phrases.pronunciation: nay het spayt mer ver zayn fol-kher-bookt foor fa-naa-font
phrases.translation: No, I'm sorry, we are fully booked for tonight.

phrases.dutch: Kunt u wachten bij de bar? Over 10 minuten komt een tafel vrij.
phrases.pronunciation: kunt uw vakh-tern bay der bar. oo-fer teen mi-nuw-tern komt em taa-ferl fray
phrases.translation: Could you wait at the bar? There will be a table free in ten minutes.

text: As soon as you sit down at your table the waiter will come and bring your menu. In case you haven't got anything to drink yet, he will ask you first what you would like. While you are studying the menu, you'll get your drink.
Talkin' the Talk
Marcel and Raymond enter the new restaurant where Marcel has reserved a table.

lines.speaker: Marcel
lines.dutch: Goedenavond, mijn naam is Westendorp. Ik heb een tafel gereserveerd voor twee personen.
lines.pronunciation: khoo-dern-aa-font mayn naam is ves-tern-dorp. ik hep em taa-ferl kher-ray-ser-vayrt foor tvay per-soa-nern
lines.translation: Good evening, my name is Westendorp. I reserved a table for two persons.

lines.speaker: Waiter
lines.dutch: Goedenavond, gaat u hier zitten. Kan ik uw jassen aannemen?
lines.pronunciation: khoo-dern-aa-font khaat uw heer zi-tern. kan ik uw ya-sern aan-nay-mern
lines.translation: Good evening. Please sit down here. Can I take your coats?

lines.speaker: Marcel
lines.dutch: Kunnen we misschien die tafel naast het raam krijgen?
lines.pronunciation: kuh-nern ver mis-kheen dee taa-ferl naast het raam kray-khern
lines.translation: Could we have that table near the window please?

lines.speaker: Waiter
lines.dutch: Jazeker, geen probleem. Gaat u zitten en ik breng u de menukaart.
lines.pronunciation: yaa-zay-ker, kheen pro-blaym. khaat uw zi-tern en ik breng uw der mer-nuw-kaart
lines.translation: Yes, of course, no problem. Please sit down and I'll bring you the menu.

text: Getting what you want: the verb 'willen'
The easiest way to tell what you want is to say: ik wil (I want). The present tense of willen is regular.
Ordering something special: 'graag'

It's okay to say ik wil (ik vil) (I want). However, you are much more polite when you add the word graag (khraakh) (it means something like 'please' or 'would like'). So you could say ik wil tomatensoep (ik vil too-maa-tern-soop) but the waiter will be more helpful when you say ik wil graag tomatensoep (ik vil khraakh too-maa-tern-soop) (I would like tomato soup). Ik wil graag een biertje (ik vil khraakh em beer-tyer) (I want a beer, please) is a good start to a nice evening!
A way to order urgently but politely is: Geeft u mij alstublieft eerst een biertje (khayft uw may alstuw-bleeft ayrst em beer-tyer) (Please, give me a beer first).
Do you want to be even more polite? In this case, don't say ik wil in the present tense, but use the same verb in the past tense together with please: ik wilde graag (ik vil-der khraakh).

phrases.translation: I would like tomato soup please.
I would like the mixed salad please.

text: Beware! Some joker might answer you En nu niet meer? (en nuw neet mayr) (And now you don't want it any more?)
What's on the Menu?
Now the time has come to choose. What is on the menu depends of course on the kind of restaurant that you have chosen.
As the Netherlands is a small country with many means of communication, not many regional dishes are left. You'll find more regional specialties in sweet stores than in restaurants!
Having breakfast or not: that's the question
Dutch hotels will always offer you a breakfast. You might be offered the following things:
Dutch breakfast is generally a light meal. Your egg will be boiled, unless you ask for een omelet (em oo-mer-let) (an omelet) or roerei (roo-ray) (scrambled eggs).
Lunch strolling: to catch a flying bird

As soon as you're going to work in the Netherlands you will get acquainted with Dutch lunch habits. For most Dutch people lunch means nothing else but a simple bread roll and a short break. In towns a lunch stroll may be attractive. Big companies have canteens and if not, spending the lunch break is a personal thing – some people play a computer game, others make an urgent call home. In business working lunches may provide good food, but no relaxation. Canteens at companies, schools, and hospitals serve:

phrases.translation: fried bacon and eggs served on slices of bread
the toasted ham and cheese sandwich

text: Taking Your Time for Dinner

While breakfast and lunch are meals of minor importance for most Dutch people, dinner is not. Though dinner at home could be simple, when you're going to a restaurant you should take your time: one hour and a half or two hours at least, depending on the number of staff, the day of the week, and the kind of restaurant that you're visiting.

In countries such as France and Spain dinners always consist of three or more dishes. In the Netherlands, when you have dinner in a restaurant, you can take two or three courses: either a starter and the main dish, or the main dish, and a dessert. In most restaurants the main dish will not come before your companions have finished their starters, but generally, you can already have coffee or tea while the others are still having dessert. Coffee and tea for the others will come very soon after their desserts.
Starters
Soups and salads serve as starters. Here is a selection of Dutch soups that you can find on the menus:

Main dishes

Traditional Dutch dishes consist of meat and boiled or fried potatoes. Additional vegetables will be served. Sometimes, salad is included, but generally salad has to be ordered separately. Desserts
Dutch restaurants commonly offer many dishes as nagerecht (naa-kherrehkt) including the following:

text: Another possibility is to have pastry with coffee or tea.
Drinks

When it comes to ordering water (vaa-ter) (water), spa or mineraalwater (mee-ner-aal-vaa-ter) (mineral water) you have the choice between the carbonated or non-carbonated water. The waiter or waitress will ask you: Met of zonder koolzuur? (met of zon-der kool-zuur) (carbonated or non-carbonated water?) or Met of zonder prik? (met of zon-der prik) (with or without bubbles?).
Wine is usually offered by een fles (erm fles) (a bottle), een karaf (erm kaa-raf) (a carafe) or een glas (erm khlahs) (a glass).

text: Talkin' the Talk
Marcel and Raymond have just sat down. The waiter brings them the menu and says:

lines.dutch: Kan ik u iets te drinken brengen terwijl u uw keuze maakt?

lines.translation: Can I bring you something to drink while you are making your choice?

lines.speaker: Marcel
lines.dutch: Ja, ik wil graag een glas bier.
lines.pronunciation: yaa ik vil khraakh em khlahs beer
lines.translation: Yes please, I would like a glass of beer

lines.speaker: Waiter
lines.dutch: Bier van de tap? We hebben gewoon bier en witbier.
lines.pronunciation: beer fan der tap? ver heh-bern kher-yoan beer en vit-beer
lines.translation: Draft beer? We have lager and white beer.

lines.speaker: Marcel
lines.dutch: Witbier graag.
lines.pronunciation: vit-beer khraakh
lines.translation: White beer, please.

lines.speaker: Waiter
lines.dutch: En wat mag het voor u zijn?
lines.pronunciation: en vat makh het foor uw zayn?
lines.translation: What would you like?

lines.speaker: Raymond
lines.dutch: Ik wil graag een glas droge rode wijn.
lines.pronunciation: ik vil khraakh em khlahs droa-kher roo-der vayn
lines.translation: I would like a glass of dry red wine.

phrases.translation: a glass of dry red wine

text: Ordering something unusual
You may need the following phrases to order something a little out of the ordinary:

phrases.translation: Have you got something without pork?
Have you got dishes for diabetics?
Have you got portions for children?

text: Handling the routine question

Halfway through dinner the waiter will come to you and ask: Is alles naar wens? (is ahlers naar vens) (Is everything to your liking?). If you wish for anything special this is the moment to say what you want. If everything is to your liking the routine answer is: Dank u, alles is in orde (dank uw ahlers is in or-der) (Thank you, everything is fine).

Being polite: the verb 'mogen'. Mogen (to be allowed) is a verb that makes you sound more polite. In the single forms of the present tense the o changes to an a. Conjugation: ik mag (ik makh), jij mag (yay makh), hij/zij/het mag (hay/zay/het makh), wij mogen (vay moa-khern), jullie mogen (yuw-lee moa-khern), zij mogen (zay moa-khern). You can use this verb to ask the following questions: Mag ik een glas bier? (makh ik erm khlahs beer) (May I have a glass of beer?), Mag ik een glas wijn? (makh ik erm khlahs vayn) (May I have a glass of wine?), Mag je hier roken? (makh yer heer roa-kern) (Is it allowed to smoke here?)

After you have finished the main dish, the waiter may drop by again and ask: Heeft het gesmaakt? (hayft het kher-smaakt) (Did you enjoy your meal?). Now is the moment to be critical if you feel you need to be and you might say: Nou, het vlees was een beetje aan de rauwe kant. (now het vlays was em bay-tyer aan der rau-wer kant) (Well, the meat was a bit rare). The waiter may react: Dat had u eerder moeten zeggen, dan hadden we u een medium gebracht. (dat hat uw oy-der moo-tern zeh-khern dan had-ern ver uw em may-dee-um kher-brahkt) (You should have told us before, we would have brought you a medium). If you are happy with the meal or don't want to make any fuss, you say: Dank u, goed (dank uw khoot) (Thank you, good), or, a bit stronger: Dank u, erg goed (dank uw ehrkh khoot) (very well) or, even more enthusiastic: Dank u, uitstekend (dank uw ooit-stay-kern) (excellent). You can also fit these words in a sentence: Dank u, het heeft erg goed gesmaakt (dank uw het hayft ehrkh khoot kher-smaakt) (Thank you, we enjoyed it a lot).

Smoking in restaurants. Under Dutch law, you are no longer allowed to smoke in public buildings. In train stations you are only allowed to smoke near special poles, to be used as ashtrays, on the platform. In offices and industrial buildings, smoking is only allowed outside or, when inside, in a special room with an extractor fan. Restaurants and some bars have a smoking and non-smoking part. In most smaller bars you can light up anywhere.
The bill, please
The waiters in Dutch restaurants don't want you to stand up and go to the cash register and pay. You should ask the waiter for de rekening (the bill) and you can do that in the following ways:

You can pay together – Alles bij elkaar graag (a-les bay el-kaar khraakh) (Everything together, please.) – or you can go Dutch and pay separately – Wij willen graag apart afrekenen. (vay vi-lern khraakh a-part a-fray-ker-nern) (We would like to pay separately).
Talkin' the Talk
Marcel and Raymond have enjoyed their meal. They are ready for the bill and they plan to tip the waiter.

lines.speaker: Marcel
lines.dutch: Ober, de rekening graag.
lines.pronunciation: oo-ber der ray-ker-ning khraakh
lines.translation: Waiter, the bill please.

lines.speaker: Waiter
lines.dutch: Alstublieft.
lines.pronunciation: al-stuw-bleeft
lines.translation: Here you are.

text: Marcel takes the bill and has a glance. It is e 82. Marcel lays down e 90. on the saucer and says: Het is OK zo (That's all right).

lines.speaker: Waiter
lines.dutch: Dank u, een fijne avond nog.
lines.pronunciation: dank uw em fay-ner aa-font nokh
lines.translation: Thank you, and have a nice evening.

text: Tipping. While tipping was abolished by law many years ago, most people will feel the need to leave a tip. After you have made clear to the waiter that you want to pay, you will have to wait. Very often the bill still has to be made and the waiter will serve some other tables before he brings you the bill, laying carefully folded on a saucer. If you are paying cash and the waiter has to go for change, you can say: Maak er ... van (maak ehr ... fan) (Make it ...), offering him a tip of 8 to 10 percent. If you have the exact money, just round up the sum of money you are paying with to 8 or 10 per cent. The phrase Zo is het goed (zoa is het khoot) or Het is OK zo (het is oo-kay zoa) (Keep the change) lets the waiter know that the sum added on to the bill is his tip. When you are paying with a credit card, you have to sign for the amount that is on your cash register slip. In case you have no cash, you should tell the waiter the total amount of the cash register slip before he makes it, saying: Maak er e ... van (maak ehr ... u-roa fan) (Make it e ...). Otherwise you can leave your tip on the saucer.
Your Own Restaurant at Home: Take-away Food

If you don't feel like cooking, look for an afhaalchinees (a-fhaal-shee-nays) (Chinese takeaway). Almost all Chinese-Indonesian restaurants offer the opportunity to take out food. You can have your restaurant meal at home! Did you miss the train station supermarket or is the avondwinkel (aa-font-vink-erl) (night shops in some big towns that offer snacks and fastfood) closed tonight? Call een pizzakoerier (erm pee-saa-koo-reer) (a pizza delivery-er) for a pizza (pee-saa) (pizza) or spare ribs (spehr-rips) (spare ribs).
Separating your verbs. The take-away food verb: 'meenemen'

When you've made your choice in a restaurant you might say to your partner, while studying the menu: Ik neem tomatensoep (ik naym too-maa-tern-soop) (I'll take tomato soup). You can use the same phrase telling the waiter what you want to have: Ik neem tomatensoep and mijn partner neemt meloen met ham (ik naym too-maa-tern-soop en mayn part-ner naymt mer-loon met ham) (I'll take tomato soup and my partner melon with ham).

The verb nemen (nay-mern) means to take. When preceded by the little word or prefix mee (may) (along), you get the verb meenemen (may-nay-mern) (to take away, but also: to bring along). Dutch has a lot of verbs that start with a stressed syllable, generally a preposition such as op- (op), aan- (aan), uit- (oyt): opbellen (op-beh-lern) (to give a ring), aanraken (aan-raa-kern) (to touch), uitkleden (oyt-klay-dern) (to undress). In the present tense, these separable verbs are divided in two parts. Here is meenemen:
Another example is the verb aanraken (aan-raa-kern) (to touch):

Sometimes interposing can be complicating. When you call your partner and tell him that after work you intend to go to the afhaalchinees (a-fhaal-shee-nays) (Chinese takeaway) in order to get some bami (fried noodles), you say: Ik neem bami mee (ik naym baa-mee may) (I'll bring noodles [with me]). You ask your partner to bring something from the station store: Neem jij een toetje mee? (naym yay em too-tyer may) (Will you bring a dessert [with you]?).

Scheidbare werkwoorden (skhayt-baa-rer verk-vooar-dern) (separable verbs) are separated in the present tense and in the past tense. However, you don't separate them in the present perfect. For separable verbs in the past tense see chapter 13, for separable verbs in the present perfect see chapter 8.
Shopping for Food
Sometimes you might not feel like eating out and might prefer to do the cooking yourself. The first thing to know is where to go for shopping.
Where to get your food?
The following is a list of stores where you might want to shop:

You will find supermarkets anywhere – every buurt (buwrt) (neighbourhood) has one. When you are in the centre of a large city such as Amsterdam, Rotterdam or The Hague you won't find many of them. Look for them at the train stations!
Finding what you are looking for
The following is a list of typical foods you might buy:
Paying and getting change back

In supermarkets, the most usual way of paying is pinnen (pi-nern) (to pay by switch or debit card). You will see the signs PIN everywhere. Only switch cards of Dutch banks are valid! Credit cards are accepted only by very big supermarkets. In case you pay cash, the cashier might ask you:

phrases.translation: Do you have the exact amount ready?

phrases.dutch: Heeft u er misschien een euro bij?
phrases.pronunciation: hayft uw er mis-kheen em uroa bay
phrases.translation: Have you got an extra euro?

text: And you could answer:

phrases.dutch: Het spijt me, ik heb niet kleiner.
phrases.pronunciation: het spayt mer ik hep neet klay-ner
phrases.translation: I'm sorry, I haven't got any change.

phrases.dutch: Het spijt me, ik heb helemaal geen kleingeld.
phrases.pronunciation: het spayt mer ik hep hay-ter-maal khayn klayn-gelt
phrases.translation: I am sorry, I haven't got any change at all.

text: Cashing the question: bonnetje erbij?

Then, after you have paid, the cashier will ask you one of the following questions: Wilt u de bon erbij? (vilt uw der bon er-bay) or more informal Bonnetje erbij? (bo-ner-tyer er-bay) (Do you want to have the receipt?)

As Dutch people are very fond of zegels sparen (zay-kherls spaa-rem) (to collect trade stamps for money or goods) the cashier might ask you: Spaart u zegels? (spaart uw zay-kherls) (Do you collect trade stamps?) or Zegels erbij? (zay-kherls er-bay) (Do you want trade stamps?).

A lot of shops and gas stations ask their clients for a plastic card in order to collect points that are good for money or goods. One of the most famous is the Air Miles Card. The cashier will ask you: Wilt u airmiles? (vilt uw ehr-miles) (Do you want Air Miles?).
Shopping for Food at the Traditional Market

Traditional markets are held once or twice a week on the marketplaces of the smaller towns. Amsterdam has some everyday markets: the Albert Cuyp (al-bert koayp) is the most famous of them. It has many stalls with Dutch and exotic food and clothes.

In supermarkets, most of the food is pre-packed and pre-priced. Bigger supermarkets do have specialty shops for bread, cheese and sliced cold meat products. In the specialty shops and markets you'll need to ask for a certain amount or weight.
You start with: Ik wil graag (ik vil khraakh) (I would like) and then, you mention one of the following measures and weights:
After the quantity you mention the kind of food you want, without any extra words in between the quantity and the food:

phrases.dutch: Ik wil graag een kilo appels.
phrases.pronunciation: ik vil khraakh erm kee-loa a-perls

phrases.dutch: Ik wil graag een pond kaas.
phrases.pronunciation: ik vil khraakh erm pont kaas

text: Handling the question: mag het ietsje meer zijn?

Market sellers will often try to sell you a bit more than what you ask for. This concerns especially fresh food that has to be sold out before the end of the market day. The question Mag het ietsje meer zijn? (makh het eets-yers mayr zayn) means: 'Do you mind if it's a little bit more?' Generally the seller will not mention the new price together with the overweight. If not, just ask him: Hoeveel kost het dan? (hoo-fayl kost dat dan) (How much will it cost?). If you agree, you could answer: Dat is goed (dat is khoot) (That's OK).

Bargaining about the price of food is not usual among Dutch people. Markets that are visited mostly by non-Dutch, for instance the Sunday Zwarte markt (zwar-ter markt) ('black market' or bazaar) in Beverwijk, not far from Amsterdam, have their own rules.
Talkin' the Talk
Petra Harskamp buys her fruits, cheese, fish, and flowers at the market. Today she's buying some cheese.

lines.speaker: Market vendor
lines.dutch: Goedemorgen, waarmee kan ik u helpen?
lines.pronunciation: khoo-der-mor-khern vaa-ray-may kan ik uw hel-pern
lines.translation: Good morning. Can I help you?

lines.speaker: Petra Harskamp
lines.dutch: Een pond belegen Goudse kaas graag.
lines.pronunciation: erm pont ber-lay-khern khow-ter kaas khraakh
lines.translation: Half a kilo semi-matured cheese from Gouda, please.

lines.speaker: Market vendor
lines.dutch: Ik heb hier een mooi stuk. Mag het een ietsje meer zijn? Het is 600 gram.
lines.pronunciation: ik hep heer erm moay stuhk. makh het ern eet-syer mayr zayn? het is zes-hon-derrt khram
lines.translation: I have a nice piece here. Do you mind if it's a little bit more? It's 600 grams.

lines.speaker: Petra Harskamp
lines.dutch: Dat is goed. Wat voor soort oude kaas heeft u?
lines.pronunciation: dat is khoot. vat foor soort oo-der kaas hayft uw?
lines.translation: That's okay. What kind of old cheese have you got?

lines.speaker: Market vendor
lines.dutch: Ik heb Edammer en Maaslander. Wilt u proeven?
lines.pronunciation: ik hep ay-da-mer en maas-lan-der. vilt uw proo-fern?
lines.translation: I have got Edam and Maasland cheese. You want to try some?

lines.speaker: Petra Harskamp
lines.dutch: Ja graag. Ik vind de Maaslander lekker. Hoeveel kost die?
lines.pronunciation: yaa khraakh. ik fint der maas-lan-der leh-ker. hoo-fayl kost dee?
lines.translation: Yes please. I like the Maasland cheese. How much does it cost?

lines.speaker: Market Vendor
lines.dutch: U mag dit stuk van anderhalf pond hebben voor e 8,50.
lines.pronunciation: uw makh dit stuhk fan an-der-half pont heh-bern foor akht u-roa fayf-tikh
lines.translation: You can have this piece of one pound and a half for eight and a half euros.

lines.speaker: Petra Harskamp
lines.dutch: Oké, dank u.
lines.pronunciation: oo-kay dank uw
lines.translation: Okay, thank you.

lines.speaker: Market vendor
lines.dutch: Anders nog iets?
lines.pronunciation: an-ders nokh eets
lines.translation: Anything else?

lines.speaker: Petra Harskamp
lines.dutch: Nee, dank u. Dat is het.
lines.pronunciation: nay dank uw. dat is het
lines.translation: No, thank you, that's it.

text: Say cheese. Dutch cheese is famous for its rich variety. Most cheeses bear the names of the regions they are from. Edammer (ay-da-mer) (cheese from the village Edam, just north of Amsterdam) is a small round cheese that is wrapped in red paper. Maaslander (maas-lan-der) is milder cheese, less salty. Oud Amsterdam (owt am-ster-dam) is strong and salty. Most cheeses are sold in three varieties: jong (yong) (new), belegen (ber-lay-khern) (matured) and oud (owt) (fully matured). The varieties depend on the time that cheese has riped in the kaasboerderij (kaas-boor-der-ray) (cheese farm) or kaasfabriek (kaas-fa-breek) (cheese factory). Though cheese is a traditional product because it has been made for hundreds of years in the Netherlands, every year new kinds of cheeses are produced; especially kinds that have less fat than the traditional 40 per cent or even 60 per cent.
Shopping 'til You Drop

text: Shopping in another country can be a fun part of diving into the culture and a great opportunity for rubbing elbows with the locals. If you are in the mood for one-stop shopping, you can head into the major department stores found in all the larger cities.
Most town centres are compact. You will find all the shops together in a couple of the streets, generally in a pedestrian area. A parking garage will be nearby.
Specialty shops are sometimes difficult to find: if you are looking for something very special have a look at the Internet first.
Finding the Best Places
In the larger cities are several kinds of shops, such as:
Specialty shops might include:
Note that most shops have the suffix winkel or zaak. Both words mean shop.

Most shops are open from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. Supermarkets are open from 9 a.m. to 8 p.m. One evening a week, often on Thursday or Friday, shops may stay open until 9 p.m.: koopavond (koop-ah-vond) (late opening). On Saturdays shops close at 5 p.m. In larger towns some shops are open on Sundays (generally once a month). Among them are department stores and garden centres: places where you need time to make your choice. Outside the towns, often near the main road, you'll find de meubelboulevard (muh-beul-boo-le-vaar) (furniture strip): furniture shops together with do-it-yourself shops and kitchen or bathroom showrooms. These kind of shops are not only open on Sundays, but also on public holidays. Have a look on their websites!
In very touristy places like seaside resorts, shops remain open in the evenings and the weekends during the holiday season.
When you want to know a shop's opening hours, you can ask:

phrases.translation: At what time do you close tonight?

text: Using the shopping verb: kopen

The verb kopen (koo-pern) is essential. Many words are linked with it, like te koop (ter koop) (for sale/to buy) and uitverkoop (out-fer-koop) (sale). The verb kopen is regular, but its spelling has to be adapted in order to make sure that the o remains a long vowel in all the forms of the verb.
Getting Around the Store

If you need help in finding a certain item or section in a department store, you can consult inlichtingen (in-likh-ting-ern) (the information desk). They have all the answers, or at least some of them.
If you're searching for a certain item, you can ask for it using either of the following phrases. At the end of the phrase, just fill in the plural form of the item you are looking for.
You also could use the next phrase fitting in either a plural or a singular word:

phrases.dutch: Waar kan ik de badjassen vinden?
phrases.pronunciation: vaar kan ik der bat-ya-sern fin-dern
phrases.translation: Where do I find the bathrobes?

phrases.dutch: Waar kan ik een badjas vinden?
phrases.pronunciation: vaar kan ik ern bat-yas fin-dern
phrases.translation: Where do I find a bathrobe?

text: The salesperson will either say Die verkopen we niet (der fer-koo-pern ver neet) (We don't sell those), or send you to the right department using one of the following sentences:

phrases.translation: on the first floor, American: second floor

text: When you want to nose around in a special department, you can use the phrase: Waar kan ik . . . vinden? (vaar kan ik . . . fin-dern) (Where can I find . . .?) ending it with one of the following department or feature names:
Finding out politely
When asking somebody for help, it pays to do so politely.
The most simple way of asking is Kunt u mij vertellen waar de badjassen zijn? (kuhnt uw may fer-teh-lern vaar der bat-ya-sern zayn) (Could you tell me where the bathrobes are?).

You can include the word misschien (mi-skheen). The phrase Kunt u mij misschien vertellen waar de badjassen zijn? (kuhnt uw may mi-skheen fer-teh-lern vaar der bat-ya-sern zayn) (Please, could you tell me where the bathrobes are?) is a very polite one.

In case you feel you're really disturbing somebody, say when he is talking to somebody else, you can start by excusing yourself: Sorry, kunt u mij vertellen waar de badjassen zijn? (so-ree kuhnt uw may fer-teh-lern vaar der bat-ya-sern zayn) (Sorry, could you tell me where the bathrobes are?).
Just looking around
Sometimes you just want to browse without anybody's assistance. However, store assistants may want to make sure you don't need help by saying something like:

phrases.dutch: Wilt u geholpen worden of rondkijken?
phrases.pronunciation: vilt uw kher-hol-pern vor-dern of ront-kay-kern
phrases.translation: Do you want help or do you just want to browse?
Can I offer you any help?

text: Your answer could be:

translation: Yes please, thank you.

text: In some small shops, sellers don't like you to nose around. They'll want to help you and they ask: Zoekt u iets speciaals? (zookt uw eets spay-shaals) (Are you looking for anything special?).
When all you want to do is browse, this phrase can help you to politely turn down help:

translation: I just want to look around.

text: The seller will let you know:

phrases.dutch: Natuurlijk. Zegt u het maar als u een vraag heeft.
phrases.pronunciation: na-tuur-lehk zekht uw het maar als uw ern fraakh hayft
phrases.translation: Of course. Just let me know if you need help.

phrases.dutch: Roept u me als u een vraag heeft.
phrases.pronunciation: roopt uw mer als uw ern fraakh hayft
phrases.translation: Call me if you have a question.

text: Getting help
In some situations you may want or need some assistance. In this case you may say:

dutch: Kunt u mij alstublieft helpen? Ik zoek. . .
pronunciation: kuhnt uw may als-tuw-bleeft hel-pern. ik zook
translation: Could you help me please? I'm looking for. . .

text: You may hear the following phrases:

phrases.translation: What size are you looking for?
How do you like this colour?

What's your heart's desire? Many terms for clothing are unisex, but some are usually reserved for one gender.
Some items usually meant for women include the following:

Requesting colour and size
Do you have a preference for a special colour? The names of the basic colours are:

These words are all used as adjectives, which means that they say something about the word they belong to. In de zwarte jas (der svar-ter yas) (the black coat) zwarte says something about the coat. In het blauwe T-shirt (het blow-ver tee-shert) the adjective blauwe tells you that the T-shirt is blue. If you want to find out more about how to fit adjectives into phrases and sentences, see Chapter 2.
Knowing your size

It will help you to find the right size when you know that in a lot of clothes you will find labels with different European and British sizes. Are the sizes unfamiliar to you? The next list might help you to find out the right size.
Talkin' the Talk
Petra Harskamp is in a ladies' fashion store. She wants to buy a blouse and is talking to the shop assistant.

lines.speaker: Shop assistant

lines.translation: Which colour would you like?

lines.speaker: Petra Harskamp
lines.dutch: Wit.
lines.pronunciation: vit

lines.speaker: Shop assistant
lines.dutch: Zoekt u naar iets sportiefs?

lines.translation: Are you looking for something sporty?

lines.speaker: Petra Harskamp
lines.dutch: Nee, ik zoek een geklede blouse.

lines.speaker: Petra Harskamp

lines.dutch: Hoe vindt u dit model?

lines.translation: How do you like this model?

lines.speaker: Petra Harskamp
lines.dutch: Ik vind het erg mooi.
