It's at the coffee machine that you start the day with fresh courage and will come back smiling several times a day. You don't like coffee? Try the water cooler! In some offices your colleagues might like it when you ask them:

dutch: Zal ik u/je een kopje koffie brengen?
pronunciation: zal ik uw/yer ern kop-yer ko-fee breng-ern
translation: Shall I bring you a cup of coffee?

text: Small is beautiful: the diminutive

Coffee stands for a pleasant moment in the day, a break and a chat with colleagues. The Dutch have a special word for such pleasant moments: gezellig (kher-zeh-likh). Not only a moment, but almost anything can be gezellig: an evening (out) may be een gezellige avond (ern kher-zeh-likh-ker ah-font) (an enjoyable evening), a person may be een gezellige prater (ern kher-zeh-likh-ker praa-ter) (an entertaining talker), the coffee lady may be een gezellige vrouw (ern kher-zeh-likh-ker hrou) (a sociable woman), and the room could be een gezellige kamer (ern kher-zeh-likh-ker kaa-mer) (a cosy room). People might even say it about their new lover: We hebben het zo gezellig samen (wer heh-bern het zoa kher-zeh-likh saa-mer) (We are having such a good time together).

The Dutch like to chat away pleasantly with a cup of coffee: gezellig kletsen met een kopje koffie (kher-zeh-likh klet-sern met ern kop-yer ko-fee). In order to emphasise gezelligheid the Dutch use a lot of diminutives:

phrases.dutch: een ritje in uw nieuwe auto
phrases.pronunciation: ern rit-yer in uw nee-wer ow-tow
phrases.translation: a ride in your new car

text: Generally, you just add -je to a word that ends with a consonant:
Words that end in l, n, w, r, u or a vowel (a, e, i, o, u) need something extra: -tje. Adaptations in the spelling may be necessary.
after m comes -pje:
You will be surprised to hear some special diminutives, which are irregular:
Notice that all diminutives are het words!
Dealing with the Dutch

Knowing how to deal with the Dutch is not a question of language, but a question of culture. When you are in the Netherlands on a temporary basis, your working language may be English. Most Dutch speak English and some of them speak another language such as German, French or Spanish. Here are a few tips for those who are not on a business trip, but live in the Netherlands and are trying to fill cultural gaps. When you have a business meeting with a Dutchman, arrive just in time, not too early, not too late. When you're early, wait outside or in your car or somewhere else. Make sure that you can finish your appointment within an hour. If you come from far away and have to talk over important things, tell your host how much time you think you need. Avoid embarrassment and talk this over. Dutch secretaries are used to book one-hour appointments in the agendas of their bosses! Know how to meet and greet formally. Read the section about talking about your work in chapter 4. Are you coming during the daytime? Only if you are a very Important Person you will be taken out for a hot lunch! A normal Dutch lunch consists of some bread rolls and milk. In most situations, you will be offered this while business goes on: een werklunch (ern werk-luhnsh) (a working lunch).
Doen: the doing verb
Work means doing things. Like most popular verbs, doen (doon) (to do) is an irregular one.
Here are some phrases that show you how to use the verb:
Zij doet haar e-mail twee keer per dag. (zay doot haar ee-mail tway kayr per dakh) (She handles her e-mail twice a day.)
Ik doe 's ochtends het meest. (ik doo sokh-ternts het mayst) (I do most in the mornings.)
Wil je dat alsjeblieft voor me doen? (vil yer dat asher-bleeft foar mer doon) (Please, do this for me)
Maken: the making verb

Though communication is becoming more and more important in offices, production keeps playing an important role. In order to talk about production, you need the verb maken (maa-kern) (to make). It's a regular verb, but needs some changes in the spelling in order to make the a sound like a long vowel.

Vakantiedagen. Holidays are very important for Dutch employees. As there are many part-timers and most of them are women with children, school holidays cause problems for them because the parents have to take extra measures for their children when school is closed. Increasingly, more young fathers stay at home one day a week for papadag (paa-pa-dakh) (dad's day, a day in the week on which dad takes care of the children). Tweeverdieners (t-fer-dee-ners) (double income families) depend on the number of holidays the employer offers them. The legal minimum is 20 days a year, the average 23, but people in the civil services enjoy extra holidays, especially the elderly. Large companies make working with them more attractive by offering flexibility and sabbaticals. School teachers have the longest holidays: they teach forty weeks a year.

Automation not only influences all the processes in the office, it also influences the Dutch language. Increasingly more verbs originating from English have found their way in Dutch: printen (prin-term) (to print), faxen (fak-sern) (to fax), plannen (pla-nern) (to plan). Here are some useful phrases that show you how to use these English verbs in Dutch:
Ik print mijn rapport wel op de printer boven. (ik print mayn raport vel op der prin-ter boa-vern) (I'll print my report on the printer upstairs.)

Cilla faxt de getekende overeenkomst naar Nadine van Lease Consult. (si-laa faxt der kher-tayk-ker-der oa-ver-ayn-komst naar nad-dee-ner fan lees kon-sult) (Cilla will fax the signed agreement to Nadine of Lease Consult.)

Cilla plant de bespreking van Hans van der Jagt met Raymond van Dieren. (si-laa plent der ber-spray-king fan hans fan der yakht met ray-mont fan dee-rem) (Cilla plans the meeting of Hans van der Jagt and Raymond van Dieren.)
Saying hello and goodbye

How to say hello or goodbye in a company depends on the company culture and your social status. When you are among colleagues of the same level, you can say anything to them: hallo (ha-loa) (hallo), hoi (hoy) (hi), dag (dakh) (hallo) or goeiemorgen (khoo-ver-mor-khern) (good morning). When you need to be more formal, you say: goedemorgen (khoo-der-mor-khern) (good morning) and you mention the name of the person that you greet: Goedemorgen, Petra (khoo-der-mor-khern pay-traa) or Goedemorgen, mevrouw Harskamp (khoo-der-mor-khern mer-frou hars-kamp).

When you leave you can say, informally, dag! (dakh) (bye). Or, very informal, doei! (doo-ee) (bye!) and in some regions even doei doei (doo doo) (bye bye) which is very, very informal. Many greetings are either local or just used by certain social groups, like the intimate doeg (doohk), which is only used among friends. Also, in the northern part of the country, people say hoi when they leave, while hoi means 'hello' in the rest of the country. In some southern parts hoi is popular. Listen carefully to what other people say and adapt to the circumstances! Tot morgen (tot mor-khern) and prettig weekend (preh-tikh vee-kent) will be appreciated anywhere.

When you need to be formal, friendly and personal at once: Dag, Cilla (dakh si-laa), Dag, mevrouw Vermeent (dakh mer-frou fer-maynt), Tot morgen, Cilla (tot mor-khern si-laa) and Tot morgen, mevrouw Vermeent (tot mor-khern mer-frou fer-maynt) are suitable.
Dealing with Your Colleagues

Dutch companies are not very hierarchical compared to American, Japanese, German, or French companies. In case you don't work in an international company but in a Dutch one, you may observe that manners are loose and the dress code is casual. Whether you work in a Dutch company or in an international one with Dutch colleagues, remember: Dutch people don't like to be commanded! It's a deeply rooted Dutch conviction that all people are equal, even if the other wears an expensive suit and drives a beautiful car. Dutch secretaries consider themselves as the advisers of their bosses and they will be of much better help when you treat them with respect. Instead of saying: Kopieer dat voor mij (koa-pee-yayr dat foar may) (Copy that for me), you should say: Wil je dat alsjeblieft voor me kopieren? (vil yer dat als-ver-bleeft foar mer koa-pee-yay-rem) (Could you please copy this for me?). When you've got a good secretary, she plans her day herself. In this case it's even better to say: Wil je dit op een geschikt moment voor me kopieren? (vil yer dit op ern kher-skhikt moa-ment foar mer koa-pee-yay-rem) (Could you copy this for me at a convenient moment, please?).
People will work much harder when you add alsjeblieft and wil je!
Talkin' the Talk
Here is a conversation between Hans van der Jagt and his secretary Cilla Vermeent. Today Hans van der Jagt is at the office early because he has an important meeting.

lines.speaker: Hans van der Jagt
lines.dutch: Goedemorgen, Cilla.
lines.pronunciation: khoo-der-mor-khern si-laa
lines.translation: Good morning, Cilla.

lines.speaker: Cilla Vermeent
lines.dutch: Goedemorgen, Hans.
lines.pronunciation: khoo-der-mor-khern hans
lines.translation: Good morning, Hans.

lines.speaker: Hans van der Jagt
lines.dutch: Is Allan Sturney al binnen?
lines.pronunciation: is ah-lern stuur-mee al bi-nern
lines.translation: Do you know if Allan Sturney is in already?

lines.speaker: Cilla Vermeent
lines.dutch: Ja, hij staat bij de koffiemachine.
lines.pronunciation: yaa hij staat bay der ko-fee-ma-shee-ner
lines.translation: Yes, he is standing at the coffee machine.

lines.speaker: Hans van der Jagt
lines.dutch: Ik moet dringend met hem praten.
lines.pronunciation: ik moot dring-ernt met hem praa-tern
lines.translation: I have to talk to him urgently.

lines.speaker: Cilla Vermeent
lines.dutch: OK. En Raymond van Dieren van Biz Accountants heeft net gebeld.
lines.pronunciation: oa-kay. en ray-mont fan dee-rem fan biz er-known-tents hayt net kher-belt
lines.translation: Okay. And Raymond van Dieren from Biz Accountants just called.

lines.speaker: Hans van der Jagt
lines.dutch: Dank je, ik ga hem meteen bellen. Heb je tijd om deze documenten te kopieren?
lines.pronunciation: dank yer. ik khaa hem mer-tayn beh-lern. Hep yer tayt om day-zer doa-kuw-men-tern ter koa-pee-yay-rem
lines.translation: Thank you, I'll call him immediately. Have you got time to copy these documents?

lines.speaker: Cilla Vermeent
lines.dutch: Heb je ze nu of zometeen nodig?
lines.pronunciation: yaa hep yer zer nuw mer-tayn noa-dikh
lines.translation: Do you need them now or later?

lines.speaker: Hans van der Jagt
lines.dutch: Ik heb ze om vier uur nodig, dus er is geen haast bij.
lines.pronunciation: ik hep zer om feer uwr noa-dikh, dus er is khayn haast bay
lines.translation: I need them at four o'clock, so no hurry.

lines.speaker: Cilla Vermeent
lines.dutch: OK, geen probleem. Ze liggen om vier uur op je bureau.
lines.pronunciation: oa-kay khayn proa-blaym. zer li-khern om feer uwr op yer buw-roa
lines.translation: Okay, no problem. They will be on your desk at four o'clock.

text: Chapter 10
Money, Banks, and Post Offices
In This Chapter

items: Knowing what you are talking about: Die, dat, wat

text: In this chapter, you will learn how you talk about money. Whether you are speaking to someone at the bank or a friend is explaining to you how to make your way in the Dutch financial world, a pocketful of the right expressions will make you feel at ease.
Changing Money

At the airport you'll find wisselkantoren (wi-ser-kan-toa-rem) (exchange offices) that are a specialised business to accept your vreemde valuta (fraym-der faa-luu-taa) (foreign currency) and provide you with euro's (y-roas) (euros). At most banks geld wisselen (khelt vi-ser-lern) (to change money) will be easy.

You will usually find a board with the current wisselkoers (vi-serl-koors) (exchange rate) or the dagkoers (dakh-koors) (current rate, today's rate) displayed in a prominent location. Look for the column aankoop (aan-koap) and the bank employee aan de balie (aan der baa-lee) (at the counter) will either complete your transaction on the spot or send you on to the kassa (ka-saa) (the cash register).
Regardless of where you decide to change your money, transacting your business is not difficult. All you need are the following phrases:

phrases.dutch: Ik wil graag . . . in euro's wisselen.
phrases.pronunciation: ik vil khraakh . . . in yroas yi-ser-lern
phrases.translation: I would like to change . . . into euros.

text: When you change money, you may be asked for een identiteitsbewijs (ern ee-den-tee-tayts-ber-vays) (your ID) or een paspoort (ern pas-poort) (your passport). The teller will ask you:

phrases.translation: Do you have proof of identification?

text: After you have proven that you are who you say you are the teller may ask you how you want the money:

phrases.dutch: Hoe wilt u het geld hebben?
phrases.pronunciation: hoo vilt uw het khelt heb-bern
phrases.translation: How would you like to have the money?

text: Try out one of the following sample phrases:

phrases.dutch: Ik wil graag vijf bankbiljetten van 100 euro.
phrases.pronunciation: ik vil khraakh fayf bank-bil-yet-tern fan honderd yroa
phrases.translation: I'd like to have five 100 euro notes.

text: Talkin' the Talk
Kent, an American tourist in the Netherlands, heads to a bank to change money.

lines.speaker: Kent
lines.dutch: Hallo. Ik wil graag Amerikaanse dollars wisselen. Wat is de wisselkoers op dit moment?
lines.pronunciation: ha-loa. ik vil khraakh aa-may-ree-kaan-ser do-lars yi-ser-lern. vat is der yi-serl-koors op dit moa-ment
lines.translation: Good morning, I would like to change American dollars. What's the exchange rate, please?

lines.speaker: Bank employee
lines.dutch: Goedemorgen. Een ogenblikje alstublieft. U krijgt voor een dollar € 0,84.
lines.pronunciation: khoo-der-mor-khern. ern oa-khern-blik-yer als-tuw-bleeft. uw kraykht foar ern do-lar akh-tern-fayr-tikh y-roa-sent
lines.translation: Good morning. One moment please. For one US Dollar you get € 0.84.

lines.speaker: Kent
lines.dutch: Ik wil graag 200 dollar in euro's wisselen.
lines.pronunciation: ik vil khraakh tvay-hon-dert do-lar in y-roas yi-ser-lern
lines.translation: I would like to exchange 200 dollars into euros.

lines.speaker: Bank employee
lines.dutch: Geen probleem. Heeft u een identiteitsbewijs bij u?
lines.pronunciation: khayn proa-blaym. hayft uw ern ee-den-tee-tayts-ber-vays bay uw
lines.translation: No problem. Have you got an ID with you?

lines.speaker: Kent
lines.dutch: Hier is mijn paspoort.
lines.pronunciation: heer is mayn pas-poort
lines.translation: Here is my passport.

lines.speaker: Bank employee
lines.dutch: Voor 200 dollar krijgt u €168,54. Daar gaat € 2,50 aan kosten vanaf. Dat wordt dan € 166,04
lines.pronunciation: foar tvay-hon-dert do-lar kraykht uw hondert-akh-tern-zes-tikh y-roa feer-en-fayf-tikh. daar khaat tvay y-roa fayf-tikh aan kos-tern fa-naf. dat vort dan hon-dert-zes-ernzes-tikh y-roa en feer sent
lines.translation: For 200 dollars you get € 168.54, less € 2.50 costs, so that's € 166.04.

lines.speaker: Kent
lines.dutch: Dank u.
lines.pronunciation: dank uw
lines.translation: Thanks.

text: Decimal notation: The Dutch use commas to denote a decimal point. In amounts of more than 1000 the Dutch use full stops to denote the thousand column, so one thousand and sixty-six euros and four cents would be written as € 1.066,04.
PINs and Chips
All banks issue een pinpas (ern pin-pas) or betaalpas (ber-taaal-pas) (debit card).

The pinpas allows you to withdraw money directly from your bankrekening (bank-ray-ker-ning) (checking account). Geldautomaten (khelt-ou-toa-maa-tern) (Automatic Teller Machines) in order to geld opnemen (khelt-op-nay-tern) (to withdraw money) are everywhere: outside banks, inside banks, near railway stations, shopping centres, and post offices. A popular expression for geld opnemen is geld uit de muur trekken (khelt oait der muur treh-kern) (to 'pull money from the wall', withdraw money at an ATM) when you use de geldautomaat. Geldautomaten will handle cards of de Postbank (der post-bank) (the Dutch Post Office Bank) and bank systems, plus the main international banks. However, your withdrawal limit may be lower than that of your own bank and there can be extra kosten (eks-traa kos-tern) (an extra service charge).
Just look for your card symbol on the machine to ensure that it takes your type of card.

If you're lucky, the ATM will give you a choice of languages to communicate in, but just in case Dutch is your only option, you want to be prepared. A typical run-through of prompts might look like this:

Transaction completed! You should now be flush with contant geld (kon-tant khelt) (cash), unless something went wrong. The machine might be out of order, in which case you'll see the following message:

translation: Out of order.

text: The machine might spit out your card without parting with any of its bounty. In this case, you might receive the message:

translation: Your card is not valid.

text: In case the machine accepts the card, but nothing happens after you have entered your PIN code, the message could be:

translation: Invalid PIN code.

text: In a worst-case scenario: The machine swallows your card and holds it with only this message for consolation:

translation: Error. Please call . . .

text: Depending on the bank the machine will tell you the maximum amount of money you can withdraw.
Pins and chips everywhere

Contante betaling (kon-tanter ber-taa-ling) (cash payment), pinnen (pi-nern) (to pay by PIN or switch/debit card) en chippen (chip-ern) (to pay with a quick transaction card) are used for most transactions. Credit cards can be used in most of the larger chain stores but are still not as widely accepted as in the US or UK.

When you open a bank or post office account in the Netherlands, you will receive your card with een persoonlijke viercijferige code (ern persoan-ler-ker fees-ayfer-er-kher koa-der) (a personal four-digit number) that is used for all geldopnames (khelt-op-naa-mers) (withdrawals) and banktransacties (bank-trans-ak-sees) (bank transactions). In almost all cases, this number will be randomly chosen for you.

The Dutch use debit cards for paying. Each debit card has its own PIN (Personal Identification Number) code consisting of four numbers. Credit cards are less popular. People use credit cards in parking garages, restaurants and to pay things they buy on the Net.

Depending on its type, your bank card may be coupled with een creditcard (ern kreh-di-kart) (a credit card). The card belongs to een privérekening (ern pre-vay-ray-ker-ning) or een particuliere rekening (ern par-tee-kwee-lee-ray-ker-ning) (a personal account). Unless coupled to a credit card account, the value of the transaction is immediately afgeschreven (af-kher-skhray-fern) (deducted) from your account. The same card, or in some cases a separate one, can be used as an electronic wallet that you can opladen (op-laa-dern) (to charge) and used for quick transactions (chippen) (chip-ern).

Fewer and fewer people pay cash, especially in towns where carrying cash is dangerous. Shopkeepers prefer to have as little cash in their register as possible and invest in pinautomaten (pin-ou-toa-maa-tern) (cash machines). You will see the blue and white boards with the word PIN in almost all shops and even at the marketplace. In some parts of the larger towns parkeerautomaten (par-kayr-ou-toa-maa-tern) (car park ticket machines) do not accept coins, just a transaction by chip card (chip-kart).
Knowing What You Are Talking about: 'Die', 'dat', 'wat'

You are now entering the area of the relative pronouns. Just like conjunctions, relative pronouns connect two parts of the sentence. Unlike a conjunction, the pronoun belongs to a word in the first part of the sentence. This word in the first part of the sentence is called antecedent (an-ter-see-dent) (antecedent). In the first sample sentence the word die (dee) (that) is the relative pronoun of the antecedent de creditcard. De words, i.e. antecedents that have the article de, always have the relative pronoun die. Check the following examples:

phrases.translation: the credit card that has been stolen
a credit card that has been stolen
the ATM that has been fixed
an ATM that has been fixed
the boy who is in love
the boys who are in love

text: For het words the relative pronoun is dat.

phrases.translation: the child that has been born
a child that has been born
the girl who has fallen down
a girl who has fallen down

text: Plurals, including those of het words, always have de. De has the relative die. Check the following examples:

phrases.translation: the book that has been sold
the books that have been sold

text: If you don't refer to one word, but to a whole sentence, you use the relative pronoun wat.

phrases.dutch: De bank is 's avonds gesloten, wat ik niet handig vind.
phrases.pronunciation: der bank is saa-fons kher-sloa-tern vat ik neet haag-dikh fint
phrases.translation: The bank is closed in the evening, which I find inconvenient.

text: In order to find out what the antecedent exactly is in this sentence, you can turn the second part of the sentence into a question, like this: 'What do you find inconvenient?' 'The fact that the bank is closed in the evening.' The answer (the fact that the bank is closed in the evening) is the antecedent of the second part of the sentence.

phrases.dutch: Ik kreeg een fles wijn, wat een verrassing voor me was.
phrases.pronunciation: ik kraykh ern fles vayn vat ern fer-raa-sing foar mer vas
phrases.translation: I received a bottle of wine, which was a surprise for me.

text: 'What was a surprise for you?' 'The fact that I received a bottle of wine.'

phrases.dutch: Mijn fiets ging kapot, wat nogal vervelend was.
phrases.pronunciation: mayn feets khing kaa-pot vat no-khal fer-fay-lernd vas
phrases.translation: My bike broke down, which was pretty annoying.

text: 'What was pretty annoying?' 'The fact that my bike broke down.'
The relative pronoun wat is also used with the antecedents alles, iets, weinig, niets, veel. See the following sentences:

phrases.dutch: Alles wat je over wisselkoersen wilt weten, kun je vinden op internet.
phrases.pronunciation: al-lers vat yer oa-ver vi-serl-koor-sern vilt vay-tern kun yer fin-dern op in-ter-net
phrases.translation: Everything you want to know about exchange rates can be found on the Internet.

phrases.dutch: Dat is iets wat ik altijd nog eens wil leren.
phrases.pronunciation: dat is eets vat ik al-tayt nokh erns vil lay-rem
phrases.translation: This is something that I would like to learn.

phrases.dutch: Er is weinig wat hij niet heeft.
phrases.pronunciation: ehr is gay-nikh vat hay neet hayft
phrases.translation: There is hardly anything that he does not possess.

phrases.dutch: Er is niets wat ik meer haat dan in de rij staan.
phrases.pronunciation: ehr is neets vat ik mayr haat dan in der ray staan
phrases.translation: There is nothing that I hate more than queuing.

phrases.dutch: Veel van wat je niet weet, kun je vinden op internet.
phrases.pronunciation: fayl fan vat yer neet vayt kuhn yer fin-dern op in-ter-net
phrases.translation: Much of what you don't know can be found on the Internet.

text: At the Bank

If you want to open een bankrekening (ern bank-ray-ker-ning) (a bank account) with a Dutch bank, you need to show a lot of documents: a passport, of course, but also proof of residency from de Gemeentelijke Basisadministratie Persoonsgegevens (der kher-mayn-ter-ler-kher baa-sisat-mee-nee-straa-tee-per-soans-kher-khay-fern) (the GBA, which handles all registration and paperwork for your local government) and proof of income as well as your sofinummer (soa-fee-nuh-mer) (your social-fiscal/insurance/Social Security number). Non-European Union citizens require even more papers.
Internet banking

In the Netherlands 37% of the population conduct (part of) their banking on the Internet, internetbankieren (in-ter-net-ban-kee-rem). All the banks offer Internet banking facilities. They allow you to monitor and manage your rekening-courant (ray-ker-ning-roo-rant) (current account), open een spaarrekening (ern spaa-ray-ray-ker-ning) (a savings account) and geld overmaken (khelt oa-vern-maa-kern) (to transfer money). You can have a look at your tegoed (ter-khoot) (credit) any time.
'Acceptgiro' and 'automatische overschrijving'

De acceptgiro (der ak-sept-khee-roa) (bank transfer) is giving way to forms of payment by Internet. For the use of utilities and monthly services, companies will send you a bill with an acceptgiro, which you sign, and post to your bank. You fill out the number of your girorekening (khee-roo-ray-ker-ning) (Post Office Bank account) or bankrekening (bank-ray-ker-ning) (an account with a commercial bank such as ABN AMRO, ING, Rabobank or Fortis). All banks charge money for each acceptgiro they handle, so many people prefer to save costs by paying the acceptgiro electronically. Providers of utilities and renters/lessors prefer een automatische overschrijving (ern ou-toa-maa-tee-ser oa-ver-skhray-ving) (a direct debit). To do so you must get een formulier (ern for-muw-leer) (a form) from the company you want to pay, not the bank. It is usually a two-part form, with the second part held back in case you want to cancel de afschrijvingen (der af-skhray-ving-ern) (the withdrawals). After filling out the form, you post it back. It can take up to one month to process your request.
Geld opnemen (khelt op-nay-mern) (to withdraw money) at the counter in a bank is still possible but will cost you some extra money. The next phrases might be helpful:

phrases.translation: May I see your passport/banker's card?

phrases.dutch: U kunt het geld krijgen bij de kassa.
phrases.pronunciation: uw kuhnt het khelt kray-khern bay der kas
phrases.translation: You can collect the money from the cashier.

text: At the Post Office

E-mail has taken over part of the traditional brief (breef) (letter). However, de postbode (der post-boa-der) (the postman) brings us on a daily base zakelijke post (zaa-ker-ler-ker post) (business mailings), pakjes (pak-yers) (parcels), verjaardagskaarten (fer-yaar-dakhs-kaa-tern) (birthday cards), and kerstkaarten (kerst-kaa-tern) (Christmas cards).
If you want to send something to your beloved, the next phrases might help you:

phrases.translation: Where can I find a postbox/mailbox?

text: When you find the box it may read:

phrases.dutch: De volgende lichting is om 17.00 uur.
phrases.pronunciation: der fol-khen-der likh-ting is om fayf uur
phrases.translation: The next collection is at 5 p.m.

text: or

phrases.translation: Collection 2, the Monday collection, has been done.

text: If you need to be at the post office you can ask:

phrases.translation: Where is the nearest post office?

phrases.dutch: Wat zijn de openingstijden van het postkantoor?
phrases.pronunciation: vat zayn der oa-per-nings-tay dern fan het post-kan-toar
phrases.translation: What are the opening hours of the post office?

text: Some Dutch post offices have balles (baa-lees) (open counters) and some have loketten (loa-keh-tern) (closed counters). When it's crowded, it's important to queue for the right counter. The counters will have the following notices:
When it's your turn, you can ask the post office employee:

phrases.dutch: Hoeveel moet er op een briefkaart/ansichtkaart?
phrases.pronunciation: hoo-fayl moot er op ern breef-kaart/ansikh-kaart
phrases.translation: How much is a stamp for a postcard?
How much is a stamp for printed matter?
Are you going to send this by parcel post?

phrases.dutch: Hoeveel moet er op een brief/briefkaart naar Engeland/Amerika?
phrases.pronunciation: hoo-fayl moot er op ern breef/breef-kaart naar en-ger-lant/aa-may-ree-kaa
phrases.translation: How much is a stamp for a letter/postcard to Britain/America?

text: When ordering something, you could say:
In case you are a lover of filatelie (fee-laa-ter-lee) (philately), try the next phrases:

phrases.translation: Do you have any special stamps?
I'd like to have this series.

text: Of course, you know how to address a letter. On de envelop (der en-fer-lop) (the envelope) should be: de geadresseerde (der kher-a-dres-say-der) (the addressee), de straat (der straat) (the street) and het huisnummer (het hoys-nuh-mer) (the number) or the postbus (post-buhs) (the PO box), de postcode (der post-koa-der) (postal code), de stad (der stat) (the town) and, when outside the Netherlands, het land (het lant) (the country). It should also carry een postzegel (ern post-zay-kherl) (a stamp) and the name of de afzender (der af-zen-der) (the sender). You could send your letter aangetekend (aan-kher-tay-kent) (registered) or per luchtpost (pehr luhkht-post) (by air mail).
Talkin' the Talk

Cilla Vermeent is at the post office. She wants to buy the special December stamps that are used for Christmas cards. She has been queuing for a long time but when it's her turn, a lady jumps the queue.

lines.speaker: Cilla
lines.dutch: Ik ben aan de beurt, ik sta al een hele tijd te wachten.
lines.pronunciation: ik ben aan der burt ik staa al ern hay-ler tayt ter vakh-tern
lines.translation: It's my turn, I have been waiting for a long time.

lines.speaker: Lady
lines.dutch: Ik heb haast.
lines.pronunciation: ik hep haast
lines.translation: I am in a hurry.

lines.speaker: Post office employee
lines.dutch: U kunt achteraansluiten.
lines.pronunciation: uw kuhnt akh-ter-aan-sloai-tern
lines.translation: You can queue up.

lines.speaker: Post office employee
lines.dutch: Nu bent u aan de beurt.
lines.pronunciation: nuw bent uw aan der burt
lines.translation: Now it's your turn.

lines.speaker: Cilla
lines.dutch: Ik wil graag 30 decemberzegels.
lines.pronunciation: ik vil khraakh deh-r-tikh day-sem-ber-zaykherns
lines.translation: I would like 30 December stamps.

lines.speaker: Post office employee
lines.dutch: We verkopen ze in vellen van 20. Wilt u er 20 of 40?
lines.pronunciation: ver fer-koa-pern zer in feh-lern fan twin-tikh. vilt uw er twin-tikh of fayr-tikh
lines.translation: We sell them in sheets of 20. Do you want 20 or 40?

lines.speaker: Cilla
lines.dutch: Geef er maar 40.
lines.pronunciation: khayf er maar fayr-tikh
lines.translation: I'll take 40.

lines.speaker: Post office employee
lines.dutch: Wilt u een BTW-bon?
lines.pronunciation: vilt uw ern bay-tay-vay-bon
lines.translation: Do you want a receipt with VAT?

lines.speaker: Cilla
lines.dutch: Nee, dat is niet nodig, het is privé.
lines.pronunciation: nay dat is neet noa-dikh het is pree-vay
lines.translation: No thank you, they are for private use.

lines.speaker: Post office employee
lines.dutch: Wilt u pinnen?
lines.pronunciation: khaat uw pi-nern
lines.translation: Do you want to pay with your PIN card?

lines.speaker: Cilla
lines.dutch: Ja graag.
lines.pronunciation: yaa khraakh
lines.translation: Yes please.

lines.speaker: Post office employee
lines.dutch: De magnetstrip aan de andere kant graag. Ja, zo . . . U kunt nu uw code intoetsen.
lines.pronunciation: der makh-nayt-strip aan der an-der-er kant khraakh. yaa zoa. uw kuhnt nuw uw koa-der in-toot-sern
lines.translation: The magnetic strip on the other side please. Yes, like that . . . You can enter your PIN code now.

lines.speaker: Post office employee
lines.dutch: Alstublieft, uw bon en fijne feestdagen.
lines.pronunciation: als-tuw-bleeft uw bon en fay-ner fayst-daa-khern
lines.translation: Here you are, your receipt, and Merry Christmas.

text: Chapter 11: Asking for Directions

items: Going North, South, East, and West
Finding your way: rechts, links, rechtdoor
By car, by train, by bus, or by plane: gaan

text: The key to getting around is to know how to get where you're going. Before you leave, it's always a good idea to find out where your desired destination is located. Being able to ask where the train station or museum is located is a good start. But of course, you also want to understand the directions you are given – behind the church, take the first street on the left – and so on. If you are afraid you might be lost, this is the chapter that will get you back on the map.
Going North, South, East, and West
Here you'll find some other useful words to find your way. Notice that de windstreken (der uint-stray-kern) (the directions) are written with small letters in Dutch!
You combine these words with in:

phrases.dutch: Den Haag ligt in het westen.
phrases.translation: The Hague is in the West.

text: The Dutch will not use the directions when showing you the way. If you're in the centre of Amsterdam, they will not tell you that you have to go north in order to reach Zaandam. If you travel by car, they will tell you how to find the ring road A10 and to follow the signs direction Zaandam. When you've made a mistake, and you've arrived in Hoorn (which is north of Zaandam) people will not tell you to go south. They will tell you to return and take the A7 in the direction of Amsterdam. Signposting on the Dutch main roads is based on the names of big cities. If you drive without GPS, be sure to have a look at the map and make a list of road numbers and cities you have to pass before you leave!
Asking for help with directions
Luckily, it's pretty easy to ask for directions in Dutch. The secret to finding a location is the word waar (vaar) (where). The question you want to ask starts with:

translation: Where is . . . ?

text: At the end of the sentence, just supply the name of the location you're looking for. You could include any of the following:

Of course, if you're in a large town, a very general question such as 'Where is the station?' or 'Where is the church?' may be met with a puzzled look. There may be various stations and multiple churches. You need to make your questions as specific as possible. For example, if you know the proper name of the station or the church, include it in your question. Your specified questions may sound like this:

phrases.translation: Where is the Saint Nicholas church?

text: If you don't exactly know what the name is of the thing you are looking for, for instance a park, you could ask the way to the nearest park. Just insert dichtstbijzijnde (dikhtst-bay-zayn-der) (nearest) between de or het and the name of the location you are looking for. Check out a few examples of dichtstbijzijnde:

phrases.translation: Where is the nearest bus stop?
Where is the nearest train station?

text: How far is it?

In order to decide whether you want to walk to some place or take a bus or cab, you might want to find out how far away your destination is. You have a couple of options to find out if something is located in the vicinity or far away, and the key words to know are: dichtbij (dikht bay) (near) or vlakbij (flak bay) (near) and ver (fehr) (far) or ver weg (fehr vekh) (far away).
You can ask the question:

translation: Is . . . far away?

text: Just fill in the name of the location you're asking about. So, for example, if you were headed to the WTC station, you might ask someone.

dutch: Is het station WTC ver weg?
pronunciation: is het sta-shon vay-tay-say fehr vekh
translation: Is the WTC station far away?

text: The answer might be:

dutch: Nee, het station WTC is niet ver weg. Het is vlakbij.
pronunciation: nay het sta-shon vay-tay-say is neet fehr vekh. het is flak bay
translation: No, the WTC station is not far away. It's near.

text: The person you're talking to may even start to give you directions to the place you're heading for. For help in understanding directions, read the section 'Describing a Position or Location', later in this chapter.
It is also possible to say it the other way around and find out how close something is by using the word dichtbij. You can ask the question:

pronunciation: is het sta-shon vay-tay-say dikht bay
translation: Is the WTC station nearby?

text: The word dichtbij is used in the question and in the answer you will hear more often vlakbij:

dutch: Ja, het station WTC is vlakbij.
pronunciation: yaa het sta-shon vay-tay-say is flak bay
translation: Yes, the WTC station is nearby.

text: When you are looking for a place, and you don't know if there is a place like that nearby at all, you might use the following question:

dutch: Is er een station in de buurt?
pronunciation: is er ern sta-shon in der buurt
translation: Is there a train station nearby?

text: In order to say you don't know your way around you can say:

translation: I don't know my way around here.

text: If you want to be more polite, you can say:

dutch: Het spijt me, ik ben hier niet bekend.
pronunciation: het spayt mer ik ben heer neet ber-kent
translation: Sorry, I don't know my way around here.

text: Going 'hier' and 'daar'

The words hier (heer) (here) and daar (daar) (there) often play an important part in communicating directions. They make directions just a little more specific. Look at the following sentences to see how hier and daar work in directions:

phrases.dutch: Het station is hier niet ver vandaan.
phrases.pronunciation: het saa-shon is heer neet fehr fan-daan
phrases.translation: The train station is not far from here.

phrases.dutch: De bushalte Rembrandtstraat is hier niet ver vandaan.
phrases.pronunciation: der buhs-hal-ter rem-brant-straat is heer neet fehr fan-daan
phrases.translation: The bus stop Rembrandtstraat is not far from here.

text: Common expressions you might hear are:
Other possible combinations are:
Asking how to get there
When you want to ask 'How do I get there?' you use the verb komen (koa-mern) (to come), which means both 'to come' and when used with a preposition 'to get there'.
You conjugate komen like this:
The basic form of the question (How do I get to?) is:

translation: How do I get to . . .

text: To finish the rest of the sentence, you need to use a preposition, like in:

dutch: Hoe kom ik in het centrum?
pronunciation: hoo kom ik in het sen-truhm
translation: How do I get to the centre?

text: or

translation: How do I get to Zaandam?

text: Describing a Position or a Location

After you ask for directions, you must be ready to understand the possible answers. Is very common to express location of place in relation to a well-known landmark or location. In this case your helper will use one of the following prepositions:
You might hear one of the following sentences:

phrases.dutch: U gaat voor het park rechtsaf.
phrases.pronunciation: uu khaat foar het park rekhts-af
phrases.translation: Before the park turn to the right.

phrases.dutch: U gaat na het park rechtsaf.
phrases.pronunciation: uu khaat naa het park rekhts-af
phrases.translation: After the park turn to the right.

phrases.dutch: U gaat bij het eerste stoplicht rechtsaf.
phrases.pronunciation: uu khaat bay het ayr-ster stop-likht rekhts-af
phrases.translation: At the first traffic lights you turn to the right.

phrases.dutch: U rijdt dan op de A7.
phrases.pronunciation: uu rayt dan op der aa zay-fern
phrases.translation: You are then driving on the A7.

phrases.dutch: U bent dan al in Zaandam.
phrases.pronunciation: uu bent dan al in zaan-dam
phrases.translation: Then you have arrived at Zaandam.

text: The preposition "to"
You use the preposition naar (naar) (to) when talking about a direction.

phrases.dutch: Hoe kom ik naar het Centraal Station?
phrases.pronunciation: hoo kom ik naar het sen-traal sta-shon
phrases.translation: How do I get to the Central Station?

phrases.dutch: Ik probeer naar het Centraal Station te komen.
phrases.pronunciation: ik pro-bayr naar het sen-traal sta-shon ter koa-mern
phrases.translation: I'm trying to get to the Central Station.

phrases.dutch: Morgen ga ik naar het strand.
phrases.pronunciation: mor-khern khaa ik naar der strat
phrases.translation: Tomorrow I'm going to the beach.

phrases.dutch: Laten we naar Den Haag gaan.

text: You'll find more information about prepositions in Chapter 2.
Talkin' the Talk

Raymond van Dieren is on a business trip to Utrecht. As both planned business meetings are in the centre of town, he took the train. The first meeting is in the morning and the other one in the afternoon. After his first meeting, he is talking to the receptionist of the company he visited. He asks her if she knows a good restaurant nearby.

lines.speaker: Raymond
lines.dutch: Mag ik u vragen: weet u een goed restaurant in de buurt? Ik heb vanavond een afspraak in het centrum.
lines.pronunciation: mahk ik uw fraa-khern vayt uw ern khoot res-toa-rant in der buurt. ik heb fa-naa-font ern af-spraak in het sen-truhm
lines.translation: Would you know a good restaurant nearby for tonight? I am meeting someone in the centre.

lines.speaker: Receptionist
lines.dutch: Op de Oude Gracht zijn veel restaurants.
lines.pronunciation: op der ow-der khrakht zayn fayl res-toa-rants
lines.translation: On the Oude Gracht are a lot of restaurants.

lines.speaker: Raymond
lines.dutch: Ik ben hier niet bekend. Hoe kom ik daar?
lines.pronunciation: ik ben heer neet ber-kent. hoo kom ik daar
lines.translation: I don't know my way around, how do I get there?

lines.speaker: Receptionist
lines.dutch: Ziet u die kerk daar? Na de kerk gaat u links. U komt dan op een plein.
lines.pronunciation: zeet uw dee kehrk daar. naa der kehrk khaat uw links. uw komt dan op ern playn
lines.translation: Do you see that church over there? After the church you go to the left. You arrive at a square.

lines.speaker: Receptionist
lines.dutch: U loopt een smal straatje door en dan bent u op de Oude Gracht.
lines.pronunciation: uw loapt ern smal straa-tyer door en dan bent uw op der ow-der khrakht
lines.translation: You walk through a narrow street and then you are on the Oude Gracht.

lines.speaker: Raymond
lines.dutch: Dus na de kerk links en na het plein moet ik door een nauw straatje. Kunt u mij misschien een restaurant aanbevelen?
lines.pronunciation: duhs na der kehrk links en naa het playn moot ik door ern now straa-tyer. kuhnt uw may mis-kheen ern res-toa-rent aan-ber-fay-lern
lines.translation: So after the church to the left and after the square I have to follow a narrow street. Could you recommend me a restaurant please?

lines.speaker: Receptionist
lines.dutch: Restaurant 'De Dom' op het Domplein is erg goed.
lines.pronunciation: res-toa-rent der dom op het dom-playn is erkh khoot
lines.translation: Restaurant 'De Dom' on the Domplein is very good.

lines.speaker: Raymond
lines.dutch: Hoe kom ik op het Domplein?
lines.pronunciation: hoo kom ik op het dom-playn
lines.translation: How do I get at the Domplein?

lines.speaker: Receptionist
lines.dutch: Dat is het plein bij de kerk.
lines.pronunciation: dat is het playn bay der kehrk
lines.translation: That's the place near the church.

lines.speaker: Raymond
lines.dutch: OK, bedankt.
lines.pronunciation: oa-kay ber-dankt
lines.translation: Okay thank you.

lines.speaker: Receptionist
lines.dutch: Graag gedaan en eet smakelijk vanavond!
lines.pronunciation: khraakh kher-daan en ayt smaa-ker-lerk fa-naa-font
lines.translation: You are welcome, and enjoy your meal tonight!

text: Finding Your Way: 'Rechts', 'links', 'rechtdoor'

Unless you tackle the words for the various directions, such as left and right, you will forever get into trouble when asking people to show you the way. Here are the words you need to understand the various directions.
Left and right
When it comes to asking or giving directions, there's no way to get around the key words links (links) (left), rechts (rekhts) (right), and rechtdoor (rekht-doar) (straight on).
If you want to express that something is located to the left or right of something else, you add the preposition van, making the following:

phrases.dutch: De kerk is links van het museum.
phrases.pronunciation: der kehrk is links fan het muw-zay-uhm
phrases.translation: The church is to the left of the museum.

phrases.dutch: Het museum is rechts van de kerk.
phrases.pronunciation: het muw-zay-uhm is rekhts fan der kehrk
phrases.translation: The museum is at the right of the church.

text: You might also hear the words aan uw linkerkant (aan uw lin-ker kant) (at your left hand ) which means the same as aan de linkerkant (aan der lin-ker kant) (at the left side) or simply links (links) (on the left):

phrases.dutch: De kerk is aan uw linkerkant
phrases.translation: The church is at your left hand

phrases.dutch: De kerk is aan de linkerkant
phrases.translation: The church is at the left side
The church is on the left

phrases.dutch: Het museum is aan uw rechterhand
phrases.pronunciation: het muw-zay-uhm is aan uw rek-ter kant
phrases.translation: The Museum is at your right hand

phrases.dutch: Het museum is aan de rechterkant
phrases.pronunciation: het muw-zay-uhm is aan der rek-ter kant
phrases.translation: The Museum is at the right side
The Museum is on the right

text: Some other expressions that come in handy:

phrases.translation: After the museum go to the left.
After the church turn to the right.

phrases.dutch: Na de kerk gaat u rechtsaf.
phrases.pronunciation: naa der kehrk khaat uw rekhts-af
phrases.translation: After the church you go to the right.

phrases.dutch: U loopt rechtdoor tot u een kerk ziet.
phrases.pronunciation: uw loapt rekht-doar tot uw ern kehrk zeet
phrases.translation: You walk straight on until you see a church.

text: Travelling by car

Walking and driving are two different things. Part of the vocabulary that you will find in this chapter can be used for both ways of getting to where you want to get. However, travelling by car brings some different terms with it. You will pass knooppunten (knoo-puhn-tern) (interchanges), rotondes (roa-ton-ders) (roundabouts), kruispunten (kroys-puhn-tern) (junctions) and you will have to leave the highway at afslag 32 (af-slakk tway-ern-der-tikhtik) (exit 32) or some other number, richting . . . (rikh-ting) (direction . . .). If you don't use GPS, but prefer to print some Dutch routeplanner (root-ter-pleh-ner) (itinerary planner) that you can find on the Internet, you might read one of the following phrases:

phrases.pronunciation: uw naymt der roa-ton-der dree kwart
phrases.translation: You take the roundabout for three quarters.

phrases.dutch: Op de rotonde neemt u de eerste rechts.
phrases.pronunciation: op der roa-ton-der naymt uw der ayr-ster rekhts
phrases.translation: At the roundabout you take the first on the right.

phrases.dutch: Vervolgens neemt u bij knooppunt de Nieuwe Meer de A10 West richting Zaandstad-Leewarden.
phrases.pronunciation: fer-vol-kherns naymt uw bay knoo-puhnt der nee-wer may der aa-ten vest rikhting zaan-stat lay-war-dern
phrases.translation: After that you take at the interchange Nieuwe Meer the A10-West direction Zaandam-Leewarden.

phrases.dutch: U gaat onder het viaduct door.
phrases.pronunciation: uw khaat on-der het fee-aa-duhkt door

phrases.translation: Across the bridge to the right.

text: Understanding where to cross and turn

When somebody is helping you to find your way, you will hear some specific verbs. Afslaan (af-slaan) (to turn) is always combined with links or rechts. As afslaan is a separable verb, it is separated into two parts in the present and the words rechts and links are stuck to the separated part af: u slaat rechtsaf (uw slaat rekhts-af) (you turn to the right) and u slaat linksaf (uw slaat links-af) (you turn to the left).

phrases.dutch: Na de kerk slaat u rechtsaf.
phrases.pronunciation: naa der kehrk slaat uw rekhts-af
phrases.translation: After the church you turn to the right.

phrases.dutch: Bij de manege slaat u linksaf.
phrases.pronunciation: bay der ma-nay-zher slaat uw links-af
phrases.translation: At the riding school you turn to the left.

text: Often you will have to oversteken (oa-ver-stay-kern) (to cross). If you are on foot you may get the instruction Steek de straat over (stayk der straht oa-ver) (cross the street) or Steek het plein over (stayk het playn oa-ver) (cross the square). Also you will be advised: Steek de brug over (stayk der bruhkh oa-ver) (cross the bridge). In combination with the bridge you might also hear: Ga de brug over (khaa der bruhkh oa-ver) (Go over the bridge). If you are going or driving in the wrong direction, you will be told U moet terug (uw moet ter-ruhkh) (you have to turn).
Doing first things first: 'eerst', 'dan', 'daarna'

If you want to find your way it's important to do the things in the right order. The words you need for this: eerst (ayrst) (first), dan (dan) or vervolgens (fer-vol-kherns) (then), and daarna (daar-naa) (after that). Check the following example:

phrases.dutch: U gaat eerst rechtdoor, dan neemt u de eerste straat rechts en daarna steekt u de brug over.
phrases.pronunciation: uw khaat ayrst rekht-doar, dan naymt uw der ayr-ster straat rekhts en daar-naa staykt uw der bruhkh oa-ver
phrases.translation: first you go straight ahead, then you take first street on the right and after that you cross the bridge.

text: Talkin' the Talk

Cilla is going to see Raymond who is in Utrecht for business. They will meet in a bar near the station. Cilla knows the name of the street and she knows that it's in the centre, but she does not know where exactly it is. She went to Utrecht by train and when leaving the station, she has to ask.

lines.speaker: Cilla
lines.dutch: Bent u hier bekend?
lines.pronunciation: bent uw heer ber-kent
lines.translation: Excuse me, do you know your way around?

lines.speaker: Man
lines.dutch: Ja, dat ben ik.
lines.pronunciation: yaa dat ben ik
lines.translation: Yes, I do.

lines.speaker: Cilla
lines.dutch: Kunt u me vertellen waar de Lange Nieuwstraat is?
lines.pronunciation: kuhnt uw mer fer-teh-lern vaar der lang-er neew-straat is
lines.translation: Could you tell me where the Lange Nieuwstraat is?

lines.speaker: Man
lines.dutch: Ja, die is vlakbij. Als u het station uitkomt, gaat u rechtsaf. Dan steekt u over en neemt de eerste straat links.
lines.pronunciation: yaa dee is flak bay. als uw het staa-shon oait-komt khaat uw rekhts-af. dan staykt uw oa-fer en naymt der ayr-ster straat links
lines.translation: Yes, that's quite near. When you leave the station, go to the right. Then you cross the street and take the first street left.

lines.speaker: Cilla
lines.dutch: Hoe heet die straat?
lines.pronunciation: hoo hayt dee straat
lines.translation: What's the name of the street?

lines.speaker: Man
lines.dutch: Dat weet ik niet. Maar hij gaat naar het centrum en je kunt hem niet missen. Daarna kruist u een gracht, dat is de Oude Gracht.
lines.pronunciation: dat vayt ik neet. maar hay khaat naar het sen-truhm en yer kuhnt hem neet mi-sern. daar-na kroist uw ern khrakht dat is der ow-der khrakht
lines.translation: I don't know, but it goes to the centre and you can't miss it. After that you cross a canal, that's the Oude Gracht.

lines.speaker: Cilla
lines.dutch: O ja, die gracht ken ik. Daar zijn allemaal terrasjes.
lines.pronunciation: oa yaa dee khrakht ken ik. daar zayn a-lermal ter-ras-yers
lines.translation: Yes, I do know that canal. There are a lot of outdoor cafés.

lines.speaker: Man
lines.dutch: Als u dan nog even rechtdoor loopt, komt u in de Lange Nieuwstraat.
lines.pronunciation: als uw dan nokh ay-fern rekht-doar loapt komt uw in der lang-er neew-straat
lines.translation: If you go straight on for a while, you'll arrive at the Lange Nieuwstraat.

lines.speaker: Cilla
lines.dutch: Hartelijk bedankt.
lines.pronunciation: har-ter-lerk ber-dankt
lines.translation: Thank you very much.

text: Coming into action

When you have asked somebody for directions, you might very well get the answer U neemt . . . (uw naymt) (You take . . .). Notice that the Dutch generally use the present tense when giving directions: U neemt . . . (uw naymt) (You take. . .), U gaat (uw khaat) (You go), and U slaat linksaf (uw slaat links-af) (You turn to the left). You will hardly ever hear imperatives like in English: take, go or turn to the left. In written instructions sometimes infinitives are used: bij het stoplicht rechtdoor rijden (bay het stop-likht rekht-doar ray-dern) (at the traffic light drive straight on), over de brug de eerste rechts nemen (oa-ver der bruhkh der ayr-ster rekhts nay-mern) (over the bridge take the first on the right).

Words such as de eerste (der ayr-ster) (the first), de tweede (der tway-der) (the second), and de derde (der dehr-der) (the third) are called ordinal numbers. They refer to a specific number in a series and answer the question: Which one? For example, to the question 'Which street?' you might use an ordinal to answer: 'The first on the left'. Find more about ordinals in Chapter 3.
Are you afraid of losing your way? No matter where you are you drive or walk, the next sentence is always useful:

translation: I have lost my way.

text: By Car, Train, Bus, or Plane: 'Gaan'

In Dutch you can use the verb gaan (khaan) (to go) for a lot of things. First, you'll find here all the forms of the present. Like almost all veelgebruikte werkwoorden (vayl-kher-broak-ter vehrk-voar-dern) (verbs that are employed a lot) the conjugation of the verb gaan is very irregular.
This verb serves you to indicate movement in a lot of situations. Here are some examples:

phrases.dutch: Ik ga vanmiddag naar Den Haag.
phrases.translation: I am going to The Hague this afternoon.

phrases.dutch: Ik ga vanmiddag naar de supermarkt.
phrases.pronunciation: ik khaa fan-mi-dakh naar der suu-per-markt
phrases.translation: I am going to the supermarket this afternoon.

text: You can use this 'to go' for any way of moving: you could go to The Hague by car, by train, by bus, by tram, by bike and even, when you live nearby, walking. The same is valid for the other two examples. If you want to say how you go, all you have to do is add some words.

phrases.dutch: Ik ga vanmiddag met de auto naar Den Haag.
phrases.pronunciation: ik khaa fan-mi-dakh met der oo-toa naar den-haakh
phrases.translation: I'm going to The Hague by car this afternoon.

phrases.dutch: Mijn dochter gaat met de bus naar school.
phrases.pronunciation: mayn dokh-ter khaat met der buhs naar skhool
phrases.translation: My daughter goes to school by bus.

phrases.dutch: Ik ga met de fiets naar de supermarkt.
phrases.pronunciation: ik khaa met der feets naar der suu-per-markt
phrases.translation: I am going to the supermarket on my bike.

text: In English, when you take the car, you use the verb to drive. You can use it in Dutch, but only when you want to mention explicitly that you are driving.

phrases.dutch: Vanmiddag rijd ik naar Den Haag.
phrases.translation: I'm driving to The Hague this afternoon.

phrases.dutch: Ik rijd vanmiddag naar de supermarkt.
phrases.pronunciation: ik rayt fan-mi-dakh naar der suu-per-markt
phrases.translation: I'm driving to the supermarket this afternoon.

text: Even when you're going by plane to some place, you can use the word 'to go'. You might say:

phrases.dutch: Volgend jaar gaan we naar Cuba.
phrases.pronunciation: fol-khert yaar khaan ver naar kuw-baa
phrases.translation: Next year we will go to Cuba.

phrases.dutch: Volgende maand ga ik naar New York.
phrases.pronunciation: fol-kher-der maant khaa ik naar noo-york
phrases.translation: I am going to New York next month.

text: When you want to make clear that you're going by plane and that you will not drive nor take the train or boat the word vliegen (flee-khern) (to fly) will come in handy.

phrases.dutch: Volgende week vlieg ik naar Madrid.
phrases.pronunciation: fol-khern-der vayk fleekh ik naar ma-drit
phrases.translation: I am flying to Madrid next week.

phrases.dutch: Volgende maand vlieg ik naar Londen.
phrases.pronunciation: fol-khern-der maant fleekh ik naar lon-dern
phrases.translation: I am flying to London next month.

text: Talkin' the Talk

Cilla Vermeent goes to visit a friend for the weekend who is on holiday in a small village in Zeeland. It's Friday night and Cilla is nearly there but she has lost her way. She stops at a petrol station in order to ask where exactly it is.

lines.speaker: Cilla
lines.dutch: Sorry, kunt u me de weg wijzen naar Oude Tonge?
lines.pronunciation: so-ree kuhnt uw mer der vekh vay-vern naar ow-der tong-er
lines.translation: I'm sorry, can you tell me the way to Oude Tonge?

lines.speaker: Employee
lines.dutch: Komt u van de A15?
lines.pronunciation: komt uw fan der aayf-teen
lines.translation: Are you coming from the A15?

lines.speaker: Cilla
lines.dutch: Ja, maar ik denk dat ik de weg kwijt ben.
lines.pronunciation: yaa maar ik denk dat ik der vekh kvayt ben
lines.translation: Yes, but I think I have lost my way.

lines.speaker: Employee
lines.dutch: U heeft de verkeerde afslag genomen. Dit is afslag 33.
lines.pronunciation: uw hayft der fer-kayr-der af-slahk kher-noa-mern. dit is af-slahk dree-ern-dehr-tikh
lines.translation: You've taken the wrong exit. This is exit 33. You have to go back to the A 15 direction Hoogvliet.

lines.speaker: Employee
lines.dutch: U moet terug naar de A15 richting Hoogvliet. Als u weer op de A15 bent, neemt u afslag 34 richting Zierikzee.
lines.pronunciation: uw moet ter-ruhkh naar der aa aayf-teen rikh-ting hoakh-fleet. als uw vayr op der aa aayf-teen bent naymt uw af-slakhe feer-ern-dehr-tikh rikh-ting zee-rik-zay
lines.translation: When you are on the A15 again, take exit 34, direction Zierikzee.

lines.speaker: Cilla
lines.dutch: Maar ik moet naar Oude Tonge.
lines.pronunciation: maar ik moot naar ow-der tong-er
lines.translation: But I have to go to Oude Tonge.

lines.speaker: Employee
lines.dutch: Ja, als u afslag 34 heeft genomen, rijdt u alsmaar richting Zierikzee. U ziet dan borden met Oude Tonge en het volgende dorp is Oude Tonge.
lines.pronunciation: yaa als uw af-slakhe feer-ern-dehr-tikh hayft kher-noa-mern rayt uw als-maar rikh-ting zee-rik-zay. uw zeet dan bor-dern met ow-der tong-er en het fol-khen-der dorp is ow-der tong-er
lines.translation: Yes, after taking exit 34, you drive on in the direction of Zierikzee. First you see the signs for Oude Tonge and the next village will be Oude Tonge.

lines.speaker: Cilla
lines.dutch: OK, ik hoop dat ik het nu vind. Hartelijk bedankt.
lines.pronunciation: oa-kay ik hoop dat ik het nuw fint. har-ter-lerk ber-dankt
lines.translation: Ok, I hope I'll find it now. Thank you very much!

lines.speaker: Employee
lines.dutch: Graag gedaan en nog een fijne avond!
lines.pronunciation: khraakh kher-daan en nokh ern fay-ner aa-font
lines.translation: You are welcome and have a nice evening!

text: Chapter 12: Staying in a Hotel
In This Chapter

items: Checking out and paying the bill

text: Regardless of whether you are travelling for business or leisure, you have to sleep somewhere. In this chapter you'll find the words and sentences that you need in order to find a hotel or a Bed and Breakfast, to make reservations, inquire about the facilities of the hotel as well as check in and out.
Looking for a Hotel

If you need assistance in finding a hotel you might want to buy a hotel guide in the bookshop. If you have the possibility, surf the Net! Of course you can find information about hotels in the tourist information, de VVV (der vay-vay-vay). Some of them offer the possibility to go online.
Perhaps you want to ask somebody you know, or persons who you meet, if they can recommend a hotel. In this case you would ask:

translation: Could/can you recommend a hotel?

text: The basic word for hotel in Dutch is het hotel (het hoa-tel) (the hotel). There are many kinds of hotels that all have their own atmosphere and level of service. Some of them are not exactly hotels and are labeled differently. Motels (moo-tels) (motels) are generally near the highway/motorway. For those who intend to stay for a longer period, een appartementenhotel (ern a-par-ter-men-tern-hoa-tel) (hotel with apartments) may offer a good solution. More adventurous people might enjoy een Bed and Breakfast (ern bet en brek-ferst) (a Bed and Breakfast): a more personal accommodation than a hotel. Een jeugdherberg (ern yuhht-hehr-berkh) (a youth hostel) is cheap and offers great opportunities for meeting other persons, but no luxury. Outside town you'll find lots of vakantiehuisjes (faa-kan-see-hoais-yers) (holiday cottages) that have to be reserved in advance. Vakantiehuisjes are generally built in parks and sometimes share accommodations like a swimming pool and a restaurant.
Reserving the room

Try to reserve your room in advance, especially during high season or when special events take place. All hotels might be fully booked! If you haven't made a reservation and you cannot find a room, you'll have a better chance outside of towns and city centres! Ask for assistance at de VVV (Tourist Office).

If necessary see Chapter 9 about telephoning before making the call for a reservation. When the hotel desk clerk picks up the phone you can say the following in order to make clear what you are calling for:

dutch: Ik wil graag een kamer reserveren.
pronunciation: ik vil khraakh een kaa-mer ray-ser-fayrern
translation: I would like to reserve a room.

text: If you want to reserve more than one room, you just have to add the number (and use the plural):

dutch: Ik wil graag twee kamers reserveren.
pronunciation: ik vil khraakh tway kaa-mers ray-ser-fayrern
translation: I would like to reserve two rooms.

text: Telling when you arrive and how long you want to stay

The person who made your reservation will probably ask you a number of questions in order to complete your reservation. You'll need numbers and dates, so you may want to read Chapter 3. One of the first questions could be:

dutch: Voor wanneer wilt u een kamer reserveren?
pronunciation: foor vaa-nayr vilt uw ern kaa-mer ray-ser-fayrern
translation: For when would you like to reserve a room?

text: or

dutch: Van wanneer tot wanneer wilt u een kamer reserveren?
pronunciation: foor vaa-nayr tot vaa-nayr vilt uw ern kaa-mer ray-ser-fayrern
translation: For what dates would you like to reserve a room?

text: In order to specify how many nights you intend to stay or for what date you want to reserve, you could say either of the following:

phrases.dutch: Ik wil een kamer reserveren voor . . . nachten.
phrases.pronunciation: ik vil ern kaa-mer ray-ser-fayrern foor nakh-tern
phrases.translation: I would like to reserve a room for . . . nights.

phrases.dutch: Ik wil graag een kamer reserveren van 2 tot 4 september.
phrases.pronunciation: ik vil khraakh ern kaa-mer ray-ser-fayrern fan tway tot feer sep-tem-ber
phrases.translation: I would like to reserve a room from the 2nd to the 4th of September.

text: Telling what kind of room you want
The person who takes your reservation will probably ask you what kind of room you would like. He or she can ask, for example:

dutch: Wat voor soort kamer wilt u hebben?
pronunciation: vat foor soart kaa-mer vilt uw heh-bern
translation: What kind of a room would you like?

text: You can take the initiative and state what kind of room you want with the phrase:

label: Ik wil graag . . . (I would like to have . . .)

phrases.dutch: een kamer op de eerste verdieping
phrases.pronunciation: ern kaa-mer op der ayr-ster fer-dee-ping
phrases.translation: a room on the first floor, American: second floor

label: Ik wil graag een kamer met . . . (I would like to have a room with . . .)

text: Wat voor een? (vat foor ern) (What kind of?). These three little words may be used by the person who is helping you, either in the hotel, in Tourist Information or in other places. This type of question helps people find out exactly what it is that you want. For example:

phrases.dutch: Wat voor een kamer wilt u?
phrases.pronunciation: vat foor ern kaa-mer vilt uw
phrases.translation: What kind of room do you want?

phrases.dutch: Wat voor een hotel zoekt u?
phrases.pronunciation: vat foor ern hoa-tel zookt uw
phrases.translation: What kind of hotel are you looking for?

phrases.dutch: Wat voor een wijn wilt u? Witte of rode?
phrases.pronunciation: vat foor ern vayn vilt uw vi-ter of roa-der
phrases.translation: What kind of wine do you wish? White or red?

text: Asking the price

You also might want to find out how much the hotel room costs. There are several options to do this. You can ask what the basic price is, but you can also ask for the price with other features included.

phrases.dutch: Hoeveel kost de kamer per nacht?
phrases.pronunciation: hoo-fayl kost der kaa-mer pehr nakht
phrases.translation: What does the room cost per night?

phrases.dutch: Hoeveel is één overnachting met ontbijt?
phrases.pronunciation: hoo-fayl is ayn oa-fer-nakh-ting met ont-bayt
phrases.translation: How much is accommodation including breakfast?

phrases.dutch: Hoeveel is een kamer met volpension?
phrases.pronunciation: hoo-fayl is ern kaa-mer met fol-pen-shon
phrases.translation: What does a room with full board cost?

phrases.dutch: Hoeveel is een kamer met halfpension?
phrases.pronunciation: hoo-fayl is ern kaa-mer met half-pen-shon
phrases.translation: How much is a room with half board?

text: Finalising the reservation
When you want to confirm the deal, you can say:

dutch: Wilt u de kamer voor mij reserveren?
pronunciation: vilt uw der kaa-mer foor mer ray-ser-fayrern
translation: Could you reserve the room for me, please?

text: Talkin' the Talk
Cilla Vermeent and her partner Rob plan to go for a long weekend to the isle of Vlieland. Cilla calls one of the hotels.

lines.speaker: Receptionist
lines.dutch: Hotel De Meeuw, goedemorgen, Ellen de Haan.
lines.pronunciation: hoa-tel der mayw khoo-der-mor-khern el-leun der haan
lines.translation: Hotel De Meeuw, good morning, Ellen de Haan speaking.

lines.speaker: Cilla
lines.dutch: Goedemorgen, met Cilla Vermeent. Heeft u een kamer vrij voor het eerste weekend van september, dus 3 en 4 september?
lines.pronunciation: khoo-der-mor-khern met si-laa fer-maynt. hayft uw ern kaa-mer fray foor het ayr-ster vee-kent fan sep-tem-ber duhs dree en feer sep-tem-ber
lines.translation: Good morning, Cilla Vermeent, have you got any rooms free for the first weekend of September, so the 3rd and 4th of September?

lines.speaker: Receptionist
lines.dutch: Eens even kijken. Wat voor kamer wilt u reserveren?
lines.pronunciation: erns ay-fern kay-kern. vat foor kaa-mer wilt uw ray-ser-fayr-ern
lines.translation: Let me see. For how many persons would you like to reserve?

lines.speaker: Cilla
lines.dutch: Ik wil een tweepersoonskamer reserveren.
lines.pronunciation: ik wil ern tway-per-soans-kaa-mer ray-ser-fayr-ern
lines.translation: I would like to reserve a double room.

lines.speaker: Receptionist
lines.dutch: U boft. We hebben precies één tweepersoonskamer over.
lines.pronunciation: uw boft. ver heh-bern prey-sees ayn tway-per-soans-kaa-mer oa-ver
lines.translation: You're lucky, we have just one double room left.

lines.speaker: Cilla
lines.dutch: Is dat een kamer met bad?
lines.pronunciation: is dat ern kaa-mer met bat
lines.translation: Does the room have a bath?

lines.speaker: Receptionist
lines.dutch: Het is een kamer met een tweepersoonsbed en met een douche. Er is geen bad. Is dat een probleem?
lines.pronunciation: het is ern kaa-mer met ern tway-per-soans-bet en met ern doosh. ehr is khayn bat. is dat ern praa-blaym
lines.translation: It's a room with a double bed and a shower. It does not have a bath. Is this a problem?

lines.speaker: Cilla
lines.dutch: Dat hangt er vanaf. Wat is de prijs voor twee nachten?
lines.pronunciation: dat hangt er-fan-af. vat is der prays foor tway nakh-tern
lines.translation: It depends. What's the price for two nights?

lines.speaker: Receptionist
lines.dutch: Voor een weekend van twee nachten is het €227,50 per persoon
lines.pronunciation: foor ern vee-kent fan tway nakh-tern is het tway-hon-dert zay-fern-tvin-tikh u-roa fayf-tikh pehr per-soan
lines.translation: For a weekend of two nights it comes to €227.50 per person

lines.speaker: Cilla
lines.dutch: O, dat is veel duurder dan ik dacht.
lines.pronunciation: oa dat is fayl duwr-der dan ik dacht
lines.translation: Oh, that's much more expensive than I expected.

lines.speaker: Receptionist
lines.dutch: We zitten nog in het hoogseizoen.
lines.pronunciation: ver zi-tern nokh in het hoakh-say-zoon
lines.translation: It's still the high season.

lines.speaker: Cilla
lines.dutch: OK, maar ik wil eerst met mijn partner overleggen.
lines.pronunciation: oa-kay maar ik vil ayrst met mayn part-ner oa-fer-leh-khern
lines.translation: Okay, but I first want to consult my partner.

lines.speaker: Receptionist
lines.dutch: Wacht niet te lang als u wilt boeken. Vanwege het mooie weer krijgen we veel telefoontjes.
lines.pronunciation: vakht neet ter lang als uw wilt boo-kern. fan-vay-khern het moay-er vayr kray-khern ver fayl tay-ler-foan-tyers
lines.translation: Because of the nice weather many people are calling to book, so don't wait too long if you want to book.

lines.speaker: Cilla
lines.dutch: Ik bel u over een halfuur terug. In ieder geval bedankt voor de informatie.
lines.pronunciation: ik bel uw oa-fer ern half-uwr ter-rukh. in ee-der kher-fal ber-dankt foor der in-for-maa-tsee
lines.translation: I'll call you back within half an hour. Anyhow, thanks for the information.

lines.speaker: Receptionist
lines.dutch: Graag gedaan. Fijne dag nog.
lines.pronunciation: khraakh kher-daan fay-ner dakh nokh
lines.translation: My pleasure. Have a nice day.

lines.speaker: Cilla
lines.dutch: Ja, hetzelfde.
lines.pronunciation: yaa het-zelf-der
lines.translation: Same to you.

text: Words to Know
Checking In
When you arrive at your hotel, you have to check in at de receptie (der rer-sep-see) (the reception desk). In order to let the receptionist know that you have reserved you say:
How long are you staying?
When you haven't reserved or when the receptionist wants to check how long you'll stay, you might hear the question:

translation: How many nights are you going to stay with us?

text: You can reply to the question how long you intend to stay with the phrase:

label: Ik blijf . . . (I am going to stay . . .)

text: Filling in the registration form

You might have to fill out een formulier (ern for-muw-leer) (a form) at the reception desk as part of the registration process. The receptionist will hand you the form, saying something like the following:

dutch: Wilt u alstublieft dit formulier invullen?
pronunciation: vilt uw al-stuw-bleeft dit for-muw-leer in-fuh-lern
translation: Please fill out this form.

text: What you have to put on the form varies. Sometimes names and addresses are sufficient, sometimes you have to fill out the following items:
When you have checked in the receptionist will let you know which room number you have:

translation: You have room number 25.

text: You will receive either an electronic 'key' (a smartcard to enter your room) or a traditional key with a hanger and the number of the room on it.

In hotels with traditional keys you have to hand over the key to the reception desk when you leave the hotel. When you come back in the hotel you obviously need the key to your room. You can ask for it with one of the following sentences:

phrases.dutch: Mag ik mijn sleutel hebben? Nummer 25.
phrases.pronunciation: makh ik mayn slu-tel heh-bern. nuh-mer fayf-ern-tvin-tikh
phrases.translation: Could I have my key? Number 25.

phrases.pronunciation: der slu-tel fan kaa-mer fayf-ern-tvin-tikh al-stuw-bleeft

text: You will probably carry luggage with you, such as een koffer (ern ko-fer) (a suitcase) or even een paar koffers (ern paar ko-fers) (several suitcases). In order to mention it all you use the word de bagage (der ba-khaa-zher) (the luggage). If you need help with your luggage the following question might be helpful:

dutch: Kan iemand mij met mijn bagage helpen?
pronunciation: kan ee-mant may met mayn ba-khaa-zher hel-pern
translation: Could anybody help me with my luggage?

text: Possessive pronouns: 'mijn', 'jouw', and the rest
Possessive pronouns tell us who owns something:

phrases.dutch: Ik heb bagage. Dat is mijn bagage.
phrases.pronunciation: ik hep ba-khaa-zher. dat is mayn ba-khaa-zher
phrases.translation: I've got luggage. That is my luggage.

phrases.dutch: Jij hebt bagage. Dat is jouw bagage.
phrases.pronunciation: yay hept ba-khaa-zher. dat is yow ba-khaa-zher
phrases.translation: You've got luggage. That is your luggage.

phrases.dutch: Hij heeft bagage. Dat is zijn bagage.
phrases.pronunciation: hay hayft ba-khaa-zher. dat is zayn ba-khaa-zher
phrases.translation: He's got luggage. That is his luggage.

phrases.dutch: Zij heeft bagage. Dat is haar bagage.
phrases.pronunciation: xay hayft ba-khaa-zher. dat is haar ba-khaa-zher
phrases.translation: She's got luggage. That is her luggage.

phrases.dutch: U heeft bagage. Dat is uw bagage.
phrases.pronunciation: uw hayft ba-khaa-zher. dat is uw ba-khaa-zher
phrases.translation: You've got luggage. That is your luggage.

phrases.dutch: Wij hebben bagage. Dat is onze bagage.
phrases.pronunciation: vay heh-bern ba-khaa-zher. dat is on-zer ba-khaa-zher
phrases.translation: We've got luggage. This is our luggage.

phrases.dutch: Jullie hebben bagage Dat is jullie bagage.
phrases.pronunciation: yuu-lee heh-bern ba-khaa-zher. dat is yuu-lee ba-khaa-zher
phrases.translation: You've got luggage. That is your luggage.

phrases.dutch: Zij hebben bagage. Dat is hun bagage.
phrases.pronunciation: zay heh-bern ba-khaa-zher. dat is huhn ba-khaa-zher
phrases.translation: They've got luggage. That is their luggage.

text: So:

Note that mijn is written with an n! You use m'n only in spoken language. Jouw ends with a w, as does uw. In written Dutch people will use jouw: Dank voor jouw mail (dank for your mail) (Thanks for your email). In spoken and informal Dutch it is common to use je: Ik heb je mailtje gelezen (ik hep yer mayl-tyer kher-lay-zern) (I've read your email). The same happens to jullie/je: in written Dutch it's correct to write: Hoe was jullie vakantie? (hoo vas yuu-lee fa-kan-see) (How was your holiday?). When you're speaking to two or more people it's quite common to say: Hoe was je vakantie? (hoo vas yer fa-kan-see) (How was your holiday?).

The personal pronoun wij has two possessive pronouns: ons and onze. In order to use them correctly, you need to know whether you're using a de-word or a het-word. De-words get onze while het-words get ons.
Extras and facilities
You might also want to find out what kind of facilities the hotel offers. Does your room have a minibar? Can you use the Internet? Does the hotel have a laundry service?
When you want to ask about specific features of your room, start with the phrase:

label: Heeft de kamer . . .? (Does the room have . . .)

text: If you just wish to sleep without being disturbed, search your room for the sign with the following message:

translation: Do not disturb

text: The hotel

Many hotels offer extra services. Usually these services are outlined in a pamphlet or menu that you find in your room. If you don't find any written information about the services, you can call the reception and ask:

translation: Does the hotel have . . .?

text: You can ask for one of the following services by finishing the sentence with one of the words:
The following questions might come in handy for inquiring about breakfast and room service:

phrases.translation: At what time is breakfast served?

text: It might be very useful if somebody can leave a message for you at the hotel. If you want to know if there are any messages for you, you ask:

dutch: Heeft iemand een boodschap voor mij achtergelaten?
pronunciation: hayft eemant ern boat-skhap foor mer akh-ter-kher-laa-tern
translation: Has anybody left a message for me?

text: Talkin' the Talk
Cilla Vermeent and her partner Rob are arriving at their hotel in Vlieland. They go to the reception in order to check in.

lines.speaker: Cilla

lines.pronunciation: khoo-der-naa-font ik ben si-laa fer-maynt. vay heh-bern ern tway-per-soans-kaa-mer kher-ray-ser-fayrt

lines.dutch: Goedenavond. U heeft een tweepersoonskamer met bad gereserveerd voor twee nachten.
lines.pronunciation: khoo-der-naa-font. uw hayft ern tway-per-soans-kaa-mer met bat kher-ray-ser-fayrt foor tway nakh-tern
lines.translation: Good evening, you reserved a double room with bath for two nights.

lines.speaker: Cilla
lines.dutch: Dat klopt.
lines.pronunciation: dat klopt
lines.translation: That's right.

lines.speaker: Receptionist
lines.dutch: Wilt u dit formulier invullen?
lines.pronunciation: vilt uw dit for-muw-leer in-fuh-lern
lines.translation: Please fill out this form.

lines.speaker: Cilla
lines.dutch: Morgen willen we gaan fietsen. Moeten we de fietsen nu reserveren?
lines.pronunciation: mor-khern vi-lern ver khaan feet-sern. moo-tern ver der feet-sern nuw ray-ser-fayr-ern
lines.translation: Tomorrow we want to go biking. Should we reserve the bikes now?

lines.speaker: Receptionist
lines.dutch: Ik reserveer nu twee fietsen voor u. U vindt ze morgen aan de achterkant van het hotel.
lines.pronunciation: ik ray-ser-fayr nuw tway feet-sern foor uw. Uw fint zer mor-khern aan der akh-ter-kant fan het hoa-tel
