lines.speaker: Cilla
lines.dutch: Mooi, dank u.
lines.pronunciation: mooy dank uw
lines.translation: Okay, thank you.

lines.speaker: Receptionist
lines.dutch: Hier is de sleutel van uw kamer, nummer 25. De kamer is op de eerste verdieping, met uitzicht op zee.
lines.pronunciation: heer is der slu-tel fan uw kaa-mer nu-mer fayf-ern-tvin-tikh. der kaa-mer is op der ayr-ster fer-dee-ping met oait-zicht op zay
lines.translation: Here is the key to your room, number 25. The room is on the first floor with a view of the sea.

lines.speaker: Cilla
lines.dutch: Hoe laat is het ontbijt?
lines.pronunciation: hoo laat is het ont-bayt
lines.translation: What time do you serve breakfast?

lines.speaker: Receptionist
lines.dutch: Van zeven tot tien.
lines.pronunciation: fan zay-fern tot teen
lines.translation: From 7 until 10 o'clock.

lines.speaker: Cilla
lines.dutch: Dank u.
lines.pronunciation: dank uw
lines.translation: Thank you.

lines.speaker: Receptionist
lines.dutch: Graag gedaan.
lines.pronunciation: khraakh kher-daan
lines.translation: You're welcome.

text: Words to Know
Checking Out and Paying the Bill

Dutch doesn't have a word for 'checking out'. It uses the semi-English word uitchecken (oait-cheh-kern). For more information about English verbs with a Dutch conjugation, see chapter 8. So if you want to know the time you have to leave the room, you ask:

dutch: Hoe laat moeten we uit de kamer zijn?
pronunciation: hoo laat moo-tern ver oait der kaa-mer sayn
translation: At what time should we have left the room?

text: To ask for the bill
When the moment has come to check out, you generally use the verb vertrekken (fer-treh-kern) (to leave). When you want to leave, you hand in your key at the reception and say:

translation: I'm leaving/we are leaving

text: After you have said this sentence, the receptionist probably will prepare your bill. And if this is not the case you can ask for the bill using the following sentence:

translation: Can I have the bill please?

text: Asking about special charges

Of course you have to pay extra for any special services that you have used. You might want to know how much the laundry service was. On the other hand you might want to let a receptionist know that you've taken something from the minibar. Here's how you do it:

phrases.translation: How much is the laundry service?

phrases.dutch: Ik heb . . . uit de minibar genomen.
phrases.pronunciation: ik hep . . . oait der mee-nee-bar kher-noa-mern
phrases.translation: I have taken . . . from the minibar.

text: Using separable verbs in the perfect and the past
Dutch has a lot of verbs that separate in two parts. They often start with a preposition such as achter-, in- or uit-:

Not all Dutch verbs that start with a preposition or another prefix are separable verbs, for instance voorkomen (for-koh-mern) (to prevent). The separable verbs are easy to recognise because they always start with a stressed syllable. Find out more about prepositions in chapter 3.
Note: these so-called separable verbs don't always separate! They do separate in the present:

Separable verbs don't separate in the perfect tense: the past participle, which you always need in order to make the perfect, consists of just one word. The following examples show you how the past participle of separable verbs is formed:

phrases.translation: to leave (behind) — Ik heb een boodschap achtergelaten. (ik hep ern boat-skhap akh-ter-kher-laa-tern) (I have left a message.)
to fill out — Ik heb het formulier ingevuld. (ik hep het for-muw-leer in-kher-fuhlt) (I have filled out the form.)
to check out — Wij hebben uitgecheckt. (ver heh-bern oait-kher-checkt) (We have checked out.)

text: So, you start with a preposition such as achter-, in-, uit-, after which follows the syllable that is typical for a Dutch past participle: ge. After ge follows the rest. This is different from a 'normal' past participle. A 'normal' past participle starts with ge-:

phrases.translation: to work — Ik heb gewerkt. (ik hep kher-verk-t) (I have worked.)
to study — Ik heb gestudeerd. (ik hep kher-stuu-dayrt) (I have studied.)

text: Separable verbs also separate in the simple past, like they do in the present:
Leaving

If you have to check out of the hotel before you continue your trip, you might want to leave your luggage at the hotel for a few hours. Most hotels have no problems with this. You might need the following phrase:

dutch: Kan ik hier de bagage achterlaten tot . . . uur?
pronunciation: kan ik heer der ba-khaa-zher akh-ter-laa-tern tot . . . uwr
translation: Could I leave the luggage here until . . . o'clock?

text: When you return later for your luggage you can say:

phrases.translation: Could I have my luggage please?
Could we have our luggage please?

text: When you're ready to go to the airport or the train station and you want the receptionist to call for a taxi, you ask:

dutch: Kunt u alstublieft een taxi bellen?
pronunciation: kuhnt uw als-tuw-bleeft ern tak-see beh-lern
translation: Could you ask for a taxi please?

text: The receptionist will need to know where you are going to before he or she can order a taxi. So, make sure you have the name of your destination at hand! The receptionist might ask you:

translation: Where are you going to?

text: Talkin' the Talk
Cilla and Rob are leaving hotel De Meeuw. They go to the reception to check out.

lines.pronunciation: na-tuwer-lerk ern oa-khern-blik-yer als-tuw-bleeft. hayft uw het naar uw zin kher-hat?

lines.speaker: Cilla

lines.pronunciation: yaa-zay-ker. ver vaa-rem erkh blay met der feet-sern fan-vay-khern het prakh-ti-kher vayr
lines.translation: Yes, we did. We were very happy with the bikes because of the beautiful weather.

lines.speaker: Receptionist
lines.dutch: Ja, u heeft geluk gehad met het weer. Heeft u nog iets uit de minibar genomen?
lines.pronunciation: yaa uw hayft kher-luhk kher-hat met het vayr. hayft uw nokh eets oait der mee-nee-bar kher-noa-mern
lines.translation: Yes, you have been lucky with the weather. Did you take anything from the minibar?

lines.speaker: Cilla
lines.dutch: Nee, maar we hebben wel extra wijn genomen bij het eten.
lines.pronunciation: nay maar ver heh-bern vel ek-stra vayn kher-noa-bern bay het ay-tern
lines.translation: No, but we ordered some extra wine during dinner.

lines.speaker: Receptionist
lines.dutch: Ja, dat heb ik doorgekregen van het restaurant. Alstublieft, hier is de rekening.
lines.pronunciation: yaa dat hep ik doar-kher-khray-khern fan het res-tow-rant. als-tuw-bleeft heer is der ray-ker-ning
lines.translation: Yes, I got that through from the restaurant. Here is the bill.

lines.speaker: Cilla
lines.dutch: Hoeveel is de huur van de fietsen?
lines.pronunciation: hoo-fayl is der huur fan der feet-sern
lines.translation: How much is the rent for the bikes?

lines.speaker: Receptionist
lines.dutch: De fietsen waren inbegrepen.
lines.pronunciation: der feet-sern vaa-renn in-ber-khray-pern
lines.translation: The bikes were included.

lines.speaker: Cilla
lines.dutch: Alstublieft.
lines.pronunciation: als-tuw-bleeft
lines.translation: Here you are.

lines.speaker: Receptionist
lines.dutch: Wilt u hier tekenen? Dank u en goede reis terug!
lines.pronunciation: vilt uw heer tay-kern. dank uw en ern khoo-der rays ter-rukh
lines.translation: Please sign here. Thank you and have a good trip home!

lines.speaker: Cilla
lines.dutch: Tot ziens!
lines.pronunciation: tot zeens

text: Using Transport
In This Chapter

items: Travelling by bus, tram, metro, or taxi

text: In this chapter you are travelling by plane, train, bus, metro, tram, and taxi. After reading this chapter you will be able to communicate with desk assistants, customs officers, car rental employees, and train and bus personnel.
At the Airport

Being at the airport, means standing in line. It starts with buying or collecting your ticket until having your luggage checked. Even when an ticket saves you the trouble of collecting your ticket, you still have to check in your luggage. In this chapter you will find the expressions for asking whether you're in the right line, at what time you leave and which is your gate.

Most airport workers speak several languages, so you can use English in case you are not going to stay long in the Netherlands. In your hand you've got het ticket (het tiket) (the ticket) and probably het retourticket (het rer-toor-ti-ket) (the return ticket) for de retourvlucht (der rer-toor-fluhkht) (the flight back). When you check in you receive your instapkaart (in-stap-kaart) (boarding card).
Getting your ticket

Unless you have printed your e-ticket yourself or received your ticket in advance by post, you'll have to collect your ticket at the airport. First you have to find the right desk. If you cannot find it, ask someone of information.

translation: Where is the ticket office/ ticket agent?

text: When you have arrived at the ticket counter, you can use the following phrases:

translation: I have come to collect my ticket.

text: After you have collected your tickets, you may want to ask: Hoe laat kan ik inchecken? (hoo laat kan ik in-cheh-kern) (At what time can I check in?). You could also ask: Hoeveel mag ik meenemen? (hoo-fayl makh ik may-nay-mern) (How much can I carry?) or Hoeveel kilo is toegestaan? (hoo-fayl kee-lo-a too-khers-taan) (How many kilos are allowed?) to confirm how much luggage you're allowed to take on the plane.
Checking in
When you check in, het grondpersoneel (het khront-pehr-soo-nayl) (the ground staff) will ask you some of the following questions:

phrases.dutch: Wilt u uw bagage op de band zetten?
phrases.pronunciation: wilt uw uw ba-khaa-zher op der bant zehtern
phrases.translation: please put your luggage on the belt.

text: When the ground staff have weighed your luggage, you could hear one of the following phrases:

phrases.translation: Your excess baggage is two kilos.

phrases.pronunciation: uw oa-fer-ba-khaa-zher taa-reef is fayf-tikh u-rou
phrases.translation: The excess baggage charge is 50 euros.

text: When the ground staff is preparing your boarding card, you might be asked the following question:
Wilt u bij het raam zitten of bij het gangpad? (wilt uw bay het raam zi-tern of bay het khang-pat) (Do you want a window seat or an aisle seat?)
In response to the question you can respond simply bij het raam (bay het raam) (near the window) or bij het gangpad (bay het khang-pat) (on the aisle), according to your preference.
You might also want to ask the following to get some details about the flight:
If you're at the airport to meet somebody who is arriving on another plane, you can ask:

dutch: Wanneer komt het vliegtuig uit Edinburgh aan?
pronunciation: va-nayr komt het fleekh-toaikh oot ed-in-buhrkh aan
translation: What time does the plane from Edinburgh arrive?

text: In case you're waiting longer than you expected, you could ask:

translation: Is the plane delayed?

text: Talkin' the Talk
Hans van der Jagt of Lease Consult is flying on business to Edinburgh. In the departure hall, he walks straight to the KLM counter in order to pick up his ticket.

lines.speaker: Hans
lines.dutch: Goedemorgen, ik kom mijn ticket ophalen.
lines.pronunciation: khoo-der-mor-khern ik kom mayn ti-ket op-haa-lern
lines.translation: Good morning, I would like to pick up my ticket.

lines.speaker: Desk assistant
lines.dutch: Uw naam alstublieft.
lines.pronunciation: uw naam als-tuw-bleeft
lines.translation: Your name, please.

lines.speaker: Hans
lines.dutch: Van der Jagt
lines.pronunciation: fan der yakht
lines.translation: Van der Jagt

lines.speaker: Desk assistant
lines.dutch: Alstublieft, meneer Van der Jagt, uw ticket naar Edinburgh, vlucht KL128. U kunt doorlopen naar de check-in balie.
lines.pronunciation: als-tuw-bleeft mer-nayr fan der yakht uw ti-ket naar eh-din-burkh fluhkht kaa-el honderd-akh-tern-tvin-tikh. uw kuhnt doar-loapern naar der check-in-baa-lee
lines.translation: Here you are, Mr Van der Jagt, your ticket to Edinburgh, flight KL128.You can go to the check-in desk now.

text: Hans arrives at the check-in desk.

lines.speaker: Ground crew
lines.dutch: Goedemorgen, heeft u bagage?
lines.pronunciation: khoo-der-mor-khern hayft uw ba-khaa-zher
lines.translation: Good morning, do you have any luggage?

lines.speaker: Hans
lines.dutch: Ik heb deze laptop als handbagage.
lines.pronunciation: ik hep day-zer lep-top als hant-ba-khaa-zher
lines.translation: I'm taking this laptop as hand luggage.

lines.speaker: Ground crew
lines.dutch: Wilt u een plaats bij het raam of bij het gangpad?
lines.pronunciation: wilt uw ern plaats bay het raam of bay het khang-pat
lines.translation: Do you want a window seat or an aisle seat?

lines.speaker: Hans
lines.dutch: Bij het raam graag.
lines.pronunciation: bay het raam khraakh
lines.translation: A window seat please.

lines.speaker: Ground crew
lines.dutch: Hier is uw instapkaart. U heeft stoel B158, bij het raam.
lines.pronunciation: heer is uw in-stap-kaart. uw hayft stool bay hondert-akh-tern-fayf-tikh bay het raam
lines.translation: Here is your boarding card. You have seat B158, a window seat.

lines.speaker: Hans
lines.dutch: Is de vlucht op tijd?
lines.pronunciation: is der fluhkht op tayt
lines.translation: Is the flight on time?

lines.speaker: Ground crew
lines.dutch: Ja, hij is op tijd. U vertrekt om 11:20 u. precies. U kunt nu meteen doorlopen naar gate 10.
lines.pronunciation: yaa hay is op tayt. uw fer-trekt om teen foar half twaalf per-sees. uw kuhnt nuw mer-tayn doar-loapern naar gayt teen.khoo-der rays
lines.translation: Yes, it is. You leave at 11.20 exactly. You can proceed directly to gate 10. Have a pleasant journey!

lines.speaker: Hans
lines.dutch: Dank u.
lines.pronunciation: dank uw
lines.translation: Thank you.

text: Passing borders: When you travel by car or train through Europe, customs clearance is totally different from the customs clearance at the airport, in particular when you arrive at the border between two countries of the Europese Unie (u-roa-pay-ser uu-nee) (European Union). The members of the European Union decided to do away with passport control between their internal borders and to abolish restrictions of imports inside the European Union. So it may happen that when you pass a border between two EU countries, you'll hardly notice it! However, you will see signs about the speed limit and different traffic signs.
Going through passport control
When you have arrived at your destination, you'll have to go through de paspoortcontrole (der pas-poort-kon-tro-ler) (the passport check).

Generally there are two lines: one for EU-onder danen (ay-uw-on-der-daa-nern) (EU citizens) and one for niet-EU-onder danen (neet-ay-uw-on-derdaa-nern) (non EU citizens). When you have passed the passport check you get your luggage and you pass through douaneafhandeling (doo-aa-ner-af-han-der-ling) (customs clearance). Your luggage can be checked here.

After having arrived at the airport of your destination, you'll naturally want to leave the airport as soon as possible. Here are some words to help you when you're going through de pascontrole (der pas-kon-tro-ler) (immigration):

phrases.translation: citizen of a country of the European Union

text: The customs officer may ask you how long you're going to stay as well as the purpose of your journey with one of the following questions:

phrases.dutch: Hoe lang blijft u in Nederland?
phrases.pronunciation: hoo lang blayft uw in nay-derlant
phrases.translation: How long do you intend to stay in Holland?

phrases.dutch: Bent u hier als toerist of voor zaken?
phrases.pronunciation: bent uw heer als too-rist of foar zaa-kern
phrases.translation: Are you here for business or pleasure?

text: You might answer with one of the following phrases:

phrases.dutch: Ik ben hier voor een vakantie.
phrases.pronunciation: ik ben heer foar ern fa-kan-see

phrases.dutch: Ik ben op doorreis naar Amerika.
phrases.pronunciation: ik ben op doar-rays naar aa-may-ree-kaa
phrases.translation: I am a transfer passenger to America.

text: Going through customs

After going through passport control, you claim your baggage and go through de douane (der doow-aa-ner) (customs), where you may have to open your bags for inspection. You can generally choose one of two options: either you queue in the line Aangifte (aan-khif-ter) (anything to declare), or you pick the line Niets aan te geven (neets aan ter khay-fern) (nothing to declare).
The customs officer might ask you:

dutch: Heeft u iets aan te geven?
pronunciation: hayft uw eets aan ter khay-fern
translation: Do you have anything to declare?

text: You could you give the following answer:

translation: I would like to declare this.

text: The customs officer might ask you to open your luggage:

dutch: Wilt u deze koffer/deze tas openmaken?
pronunciation: wilt uw day-zer ko-fer/day-zer tas oa-pern-maa-kern
translation: Please open this suitcase/this bag.

text: When the customs officer asks you what you're going to do with something you have bought you can answer:
If the custom officer does not agree with something he finds in your suitcase, he might say:

phrases.translation: It's not allowed to import this.
It's not allowed to export this.
You have to pay duty on this.

text: You could answer him with the question:

translation: How much do I owe you?

text: When you have paid your duties and you've been cleared, the customs officer will tell you: U mag doorlopen (uw makh doar-loa-pern) (You may go through).
Travelling by Car
When you are going to travel internationally in a car, make sure that you have the right driving license. You can find information on www.rdw.nl or at your local town, city or district hall.

The most important roads are called snelwegen (snel-vay-khern) (highways/ motorways). Even though these highways have four to six rijbanen (ray-baa-nern) (lanes), you'll come across many files (fee-lers) (traffic jams). You will be in them in het spitsuur (in het spits-uwr) (during rush hours) which may last until nine o'clock in the morning and start after three o'clock in the afternoon. Whenever something special takes place: een ongeluk (ern on-kher-luhk) (an accident), regen (ray-khern) (rain), mist (mist) (fog), or sneeuw (snayw) (snow), you may in de file staan (in der fee-ler staan) (to be in a traffic jam). Wegwerkzaamheden (vekh-verk-zaam-hay-dern) (road works), especially onderhoud (on-der-hout) (maintenance), generally take place in summer, during the night and weekends. Even then, you are not sure if you can doorrijden (doar-ray-dern) (drive on).
Some important highways are:

phrases.translation: which goes from West to East, from Amsterdam passing through Enschede to Germany.
which goes from North to South, from Amsterdam to Maastricht.
which goes from Amsterdam via Den Haag to Rotterdam.

text: If you want to see more of the country you can take a smaller road. Provinciale wegen (proa-fin-shaa-ler vay-khern) (provincial roads) have numbers and generally have two to four lanes. When you take them in order to avoid verkeersopstoppingen (fer-kayrs-op-sto-ping-ern) (traffic jams), you may find hundreds of cars trying a shortcut. It won't save you time. Are you driving for leisure? Try to travel between nine in the morning and three o'clock in the afternoon!
Renting a car
If you've decided to rent a car you need to make your way to een autover huurbedrijf (ern ow-toa-fer-huur-ber-drayf) (a car rental agency). Here are some useful sentences once you have arrived:

dutch: Ik wil graag een auto huren.
pronunciation: ik vil khraakh ern ow-toa huu-rem
translation: I would like to rent a car.

text: The attendant will ask you what kind of car you want, saying something like:

dutch: Wat voor soort auto wilt u huren?
pronunciation: vat foar soart ow-toa wilt uw huu-rem
translation: What kind of car would you like to rent?

text: To which you can respond with any of the following:
Generally the cars are divided into price classes. The following extras might be offered:

text: Understanding maps and road signs

Even when you have GPS, it's useful to understand maps. A good map tells you where you are, how to get there and how far you have to go. Maps are very visual and you don't need to understand a lot of Dutch in order to be able to read one. You might like to know the following different kind of maps, in case you need to ask for one:
On a road map you'll find, among other things:

phrases.translation: national roads e.g. national road N31.
secondary roads e.g. secondary road N266
filling stations that are open day and night

text: Dutch pride: the water household. On the map you may also find the icons for gemaal (kher-maal) (pumping station) and sluis (sloais) (lock). Both words are connected to the enormous water household of the Netherlands. Ages ago the name of the western part of the Netherlands was de Lage Landen (der laa-khern lan-dern) (the Lowlands). Big parts of the lowlands consisted of water. Perhaps you arrived at Schiphol Airport by plane. In this case, you landed below sea-level on the bottom of a former (man-made) lake, now called polder (pol-der) (polder). The Cruquius Gemaal (kruw-kee-yuhs kher-maal) (the pumping station named after its engineer Cruquius) pumped for three years to get the Haarlemmermeer (haar-leh-mer-mayr) (Haarlem lake), where Schiphol is, free from water. The pumping station is an industrial monument now. Nowadays every polder has an electric gemaal to keep it dry. Pleasure yachts that are sailing on the Dutch binnenwateren (bi-nern-vaa-ter-ern) (waterways) have to pass a lot of sluizen (sloai-zern) (locks) that help to overcome differences of 3 or 4 meters in levels between the water of the ring-vaarten (ring-faa-tern) (ring canals, the canals that surround a polder) and the water in the low-lying polders. Whenever you see some locks at work, make the most of your opportunity to stay a while and see how they function!

When you're driving for leisure and if you're interested in seeing special things, the icons on the map might help you to find bezienswaardigheden (ber-zens-vaar-dikh-hay-dern) (places of interest) like kastelen (kas-tay-lern) (castles) and ruines (ruu-wee-nern) (ruins). In case you're going for a hike, you'll find duinen (doai-nern) (dunes), heide (hay-der) (heath) and bos (bos) (wooded area).
For those who are on business trips: industrie terreinen (in-duhs-tree-tray-nern) (industrial areas) are well indicated.
City maps
If you want to know a town, start by buying a city map. A city map shows you not only straten (straa-tern) (streets) and pleinen (play-nern) (squares), but also:

The city map will tell you the centrum (sen-truhm) (centre) of town consists of a voetgangerszone (foot-khang-ers-zoe-ner) (pedestrian area). When you visit such a centre, leave your car on a parkeerplaats (par-kayr-plaats) (a parking lot) or in een parkeergarage (par-kayr-khaa-raa-zher) (parking garage) at the edge of the centre. The town will reveal its details while you are strolling through the centre.

In smaller towns it's possible to park your car in the centre and you'll find parkeermeters (par-kayr-may-ters) (parking meters) in which you have to geld inwerpen (khelt-in-ver-pern) (insert some coins). The inworp per uur (in-vorp pehr uur) (insertion per hour) differs from 1 to 5 op werkdagen tot 18:00 (op vehrk-daa-khern tot zes uur) (until 6 o'clock on working days) met uitzondering van feestdagen (met oat-zon-der-ring fan fayst-daa-khern) (with the exception of public holidays).

After your stroll through the centre and when you have left the parking garage, you will soon see a sign telling you: alle richtingen (a-ler rikh-ting-ern) (all directions). It brings you to de rondweg (der ront-vekh) (the ring road/ beltway) or de ring (der ring) (the ring): the road that goes around the town. It has junctions with main roads in all directions.

Large towns with historic and crowded centres will surprise you with hidden private garages even in the narrowest streets. Don't park your car on places where you see the small round red and white sign with the words uitrit vrijlaten (oa-trit fray-laa-tern) (keep exit clear).

text: Road signs

You don't want to get stopped for speeding down a one-way street going in the wrong direction. Road signs are generally visual and universal, yet some are verbal. Here are some signs that mean you shouldn't drive on, but turn back:

In de bebouwde kom (der ber-bouw-der kom) (the built-up area) de maximum-snelheid (mak-see-muhm-snel-hay) (maximum speed limit) is 50 kilometers. Many small villages which you pass through when driving on a secondary road, have flitspalen (flits-paa-lern) (flash poles), small grey boxes on a pole that photograph you when you are speeding or jumping the lights. Six weeks later, you'll receive an acceptgiro (ak-sept-khee-roa) (a bank transfer) fining you for every kilometer that you drove too fast. In case you drove 30 km too fast binnen de bebouwde kom (bi-nern der ber-bouw-der kom) (inside the built-up area), you'll have to pay 170 euro, and for speeding by 30 km on the highway, the fine will be 160 euro.

Breaking the rules. When you are on the motorway and guilty of te snel rijden (ter snel ray-dern) (speeding), geen richting aangeven (khayn rikh-ting aan-khay-vern) (failing to indicate a change of direction) or verkeerd inhalen (fer-kayrt in-haa-lern) (unauthorised overtaking) the police will fine you when they catch you doing so. The police will first pursue you and then they will overtake you and force you to stop, lighting up a sign on the car. Stop, politie (stop poa-lee-see) (stop, police). If you don't open the door of your car for the policeman, he will do it for you and he will sit on the sill of your car telling you what you did wrong and even when you say sorry, or tell him you didn't see the road sign, the story will end with a fine in excess of 100 euro.
The motorway

When you're driving on some secondary road and approach the motorway, you might meet the sign Ga terug (khaa ter-ruhkh) (go back!). You will see this sign at the end of exits of the highway that are parallel to the entrance of the highway. It's meant to protect sleepy drivers who might take the exit instead of the entrance. These spookrijders (spook-ray-ders) (motorists driving against the traffic) would meet unexpected tegenliggers (tay-khern-likh-kers) (on coming traffic).

When you're on the highway you are lucky when you see light boxes with texts like A1 filevrij (aa-an fee-ler-fray) (no tailback). It's more likely that you will read the text: A1 tot knooppunt Hoevelaken 8 kilometer file. (aa-an tot knaa-punt hoo-fer-lau-kern akht kee-loa-may-ter fee-ler) (A1 until interchange Hoevelaken eight kilometers tailback).

When you're in een opstopping (ern op-sto-ping) (a traffic jam) and you'll have to van richting veranderen (fan rikh-ting fer-an-der-ern) (change direction) it is more important than ever to invoegen (in-foo-khern) (join the traffic) in time, though you have to langzaam rijden (lang-zaam ray-dern) (drive slowly). Let's hope that you won't meet een omleiding (ern oam-lay-ding) (diversion)! In this case, it will help you to know that volg route nummer 1 (folk roa-ter nuh-mer ayn) means: follow route number one.

Are you overtaken by bad weather? In case of hagel (haa-khert) (hail): Lichten ontsteken (likh-tern ont-stay-kern) (switch on lights) and drive carefully because of slippevaar (slip-ker-faar) (slippery road)!

text: Verbs in the past tense: some irregular ones

Dutch-speaking people don't use the past tense as much as English-speaking people do. Dutch-speaking people use it when describing something, when talking about habits or when enumerating a chain of facts. The story of Raymond, on his way to Amersfoort is a chain of facts, and that's why he tells most of it in the past tense: was, moest, zat, kon, wist, and had. Raymond uses some irregular verbs. Dutch has a lot of them and, as they are irregular, they hardly follow any rules and are difficult to learn. You'll first learn the ones that are used most, just by hearing other people use them.
Let's first see how the regular past tense works. To make the past tense, take the I-form or the stem of a verb and add -de or -te:
stem + de/te
Most verbs add -de. But verbs that have a stem ending in the letters t, k, f, s, ch or p add -te. See the following examples:

A popular trick in order to remember which letters cause the verb to end in -te is the word 'T KoFSCHIP. As this word might be difficult to remember and pronounce, most English-speaking people prefer SoFT KeTCHuP as a memory aid.
Irregular verbs, however, don't follow these rules. There is no other solution than learning them by heart. Here are some frequently used verbs with an irregular past tense:
Getting to work

60% of the Dutch travel to work met de auto (met der ow-toa) (by car), 10% neemt de trein (naymt der trayn) (take the train) or some other kind of open-baar vervoer (oa-pern-baar fer-voar) (public transport), 25% gaat op de fiets (khaat op der feets) (take the bike), and only 5% of them walk. The fietsers (feetsers) (cyclists) arrive first at work: they need only 15 minutes on average. Fietsen (feet-sern) (cycling) is popular in towns and other places where distances are short. In towns cars have to wait for streams of cyclists passing by.

When you take part in Dutch traffic, you may get the impression that the majority of bikers are seriously suicidal. Although they are pretty vulnerable, many of them will not yield to a car, possibly as a matter of principle. Bikers have to indicate their direction by holding out their right or left hand, but only elderly bikers do. Jumping traffic lights is also common. Car drivers in large towns need eyes everywhere: especially when getting out of their cars. Beware when you are driving in a narrow street: bikes will pass you left and right! Look carefully before you turn to the right: cyclists can reach speeds of more than 20 km per hour and you might have missed one when you were looking in your right wing mirror.

Racefietsers (rays-fee-tsers) (racing cyclists) prefer fietspaden (feets-paa-dern) (cycle tracks) along provincial roads. Car drivers might meet groups of them on summer evenings, Saturdays, and Sundays. The sign Fietsers oversteken (feet-sers oa-fer-stay-kern) (cyclists' crossing) warns cyclists that they have to cross the road because the fietspad continues at the other side of the road. Car drivers, be alert!

A company bike keeps you fit. Absence as a result of illness is every employer's nightmare. Dutch employers have to continue paying salary during two years when an employee falls ill. Employers want their employees to be healthy, and that's why de baas (der baas) (the boss) likes it when employees go for a lunchwandeling (luhnsh-van-der-ling) (lunch walk). Big companies offer stoelmassage (stool-ma-saa-zher) (a massage when sitting in the working chair) or a reduction for the fitness-club (fit-ners-klup) (the fitness club). The law allows employers to give their employees een bedrijfsfiets (ern ber-drays-feets) (a company bike) tax-free worth 750 euro every three years. It's even possible to lease a bedrijfsfiets!
Mopeds and scooters

Young people from the age of 16 drive bromfietsen (brom-feets-ern) (mopeds) and scooters (skoo-ters) (which have a higher capacity than mopeds) especially for longer distances. In towns fietsers and bromfietsers sometimes drive on the road, sometimes on het fietspad. Brommers (bro-mers) (this is the most common word for mopeds) sometimes are, and sometimes aren't, allowed to drive on the same fietspad.

To drive a moped is rather risky: every year 75 people are killed and 2000 seriously wounded. To wear a helmet is obligatory. To wear a helmet is not compulsory for bikers. Racefietsers and mountainbikers (maun-ten-ba-kers) (cyclists on racing or mountain bikes) often do wear one. It may save their life in case of a crash.

lines.speaker: Petra

lines.translation: I have started already, but you know that I have to discuss a few things with you.

lines.speaker: Marcel

lines.pronunciation: so-ree ik stont in der fee-ler
